Country of publication: India (p. 1). Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa! Homage to Śrī Sarasvatī! Homage to the venerable Gurus! Homage to Śrī Nātha! Oṃ, homage to Brahmā and the others, the founders of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman, to the ancestral sages, and to the gurus.
We worship the elephant-faced one, the sun to the lotus of the face, who has many tusks yet appears as single-tusked to his devotees, day and night.
Having prostrated before the Guru, Gaṇapati, Vāṇī, the Lord of Ambā, and the supreme Kṣetrapati, I shall expound the *Svacchandapaddhati* for those established on the path of consciousness.
The lord of yogis named Amṛtānanda, his impurities removed through awakening,
wandered this earth as the lord of yogis known as Brahmānanda.
Having deliberated, he made his own disciple, named Vimalānanda, who was proficient in his own doctrine; from him, indeed, Cidānanda came into being.
Having realized my true nature as indivisible awareness through the awakening of consciousness-bliss, I move about;
O Lord, instruct me accordingly, so that by your grace and that of the gurus, may there be uninterrupted [realization] within you quickly.
O Sadānanda, you who are a mass of nectar and belong to the Kaulālākhyā lineage—
I bow to the Guru Cidānanda, carrying your command upon my head.
Having deliberated with supreme intelligence upon the scriptures of the family tradition (kuladharma),
I shall explain the manual of the Svachchanda for the benefit of practitioners.

Therein, the illustrious lord of practitioners, having risen at dawn during the first watch before the morning twilight—or during the fourth watch of the day, in the *brāhma-muhūrta*—being purified, should meditate upon his own Guru within the pericarp of a white thousand-petaled lotus on his own head.

Having meditated upon that form with a great mind imbued with the nectar of the glorious mass of awakening, [he should contemplate]: "I am eternally [that form], possessing the luster of the lunar orb of consciousness within the thousand-petaled [lotus]."

Having led [the deity] to that very Guru, one should contemplate and meditate upon him as the essence of the mantra within the sixteen-petaled lotus; indeed, I thus remember the Śrī Guru within the interior of the heart-lotus.
Then, having worshipped one's own Guru three times with the *pādukā* mantra using the *mṛgīmudrā*, one should recite one's own name once at the *mūlādhāra*.

Having honored the Guru, one should worship him with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). That is as follows: *Laṃ*, I offer fragrance consisting of the element earth; *Haṃ*, I offer flowers consisting of the element ether; *Yaṃ*, I offer incense consisting of the element air; *Raṃ*, I offer a lamp consisting of the element fire; *Taṃ*, [I offer] that which consists of nectar...
"I offer the food offering; I offer the betel-leaf, which is the soul of all. Having thus worshipped:
"Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whom the eyes of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance have been opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge."
Homage be to that Guru, who is the very embodiment of the chosen deity,
whose left-hand nectar destroys the poison known as saṃsāra.

Having thus prostrated with the *yonimudrā* through the realization of one's own identity [with the Guru], and meditating upon the Guru—who is non-dual with Śiva—as being Śiva himself, one should recite the hymn to the Guru:
"Salutations to you, O Lord, O Blessed One, who are Śiva in the form of the Guru;
you who have assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfectly accomplishing the descent of the *vidyā*."
Salutations to the one who is ever-new and of ever-new form, whose single nature is the ultimate reality,
who is like the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance, and who is a mass of pure consciousness.

To the one who is independent, whose form is fashioned by compassion, whose nature is auspiciousness; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in a gracious form for those who are worthy of liberation.
To the one who is the discernment for the discerning, the investigation for the investigating,
the illumination for those who illuminate, and the embodiment of knowledge for the wise.
In front, on both sides, behind, above, and below, may you always provide a seat for me by means of your form as my own mind; I shall pay homage [to you] there.

Then, having visualized one's own body being sprinkled by streams flowing from the nectar of that lotus-foot, and having recited the *pādukā-mantra* once, one should dismiss it with the words "forgive me. This is the mental worship (*mānasapūjā*) of the Guru.

Then, having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should perform yogic meditation (*yogadhyāna*). [One should meditate on the energy] extending from the root-center (*mūlakanda*) up to the staff...

One should meditate upon the Brahma-nāḍī as white in color, extending up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). In its center, one should contemplate Bhavānī, who resembles [the moon]—having emerged from the hollow of the Mūlālavāla, like a flash of lightning, she pierces the six lotuses;
then, taking the form of a rain of supreme nectar dripping from the moon of the Dhruvamaṇḍala, she enters there once again.
We behold the seal of bliss, which shines forth at the first departure, becomes like nectar upon the return journey, and moves within by abandoning its internal locations.
Upon the support, which is as radiant as the orb of the rising sun, stands the seed-syllable *vāgbhava*, possessing the luster of gold;
situated in the heart-lotus is the seed-syllable of *manmatha*, resembling an *indragopaka* insect;
and in the aperture of the station of Brahmā is the other syllable of *śakti*, brilliant with the radiance of the moon.
O Śivā, those who meditate upon your three steps attain supreme bliss.
With a concentrated mind, one should contemplate for a long time the Root-Vidyā situated in the three peaks,
as slender as a lotus fiber, extending from the base of the spine to the aperture of Brahmā.
One should contemplate [the Goddess] upon one's own body, radiant with the splendor of the rising sun.
Such is the application of the mantra.
For this glorious Great Mantra of the Sixteen Syllables of Śrīvidyā, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), and she whose nature is the sixfold [Śrīvidyā] is the deity.

The deity is Mahātripurasundarī; *aiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *sauḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *klīṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of attaining the grace of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī through recitation (*japa*). Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*):
On the head: Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer (ṛṣi). In the mouth: [Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ], salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas).
In the heart: [Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ], salutation to the deity Śrī Mahātripurasundarī.
On the right breast—4 *aiṃ* to the Seed-syllable (*bīja*), salutation; on the left breast—4 *sauṃ* to the Power (*śakti*), salutation;
at the navel—4 *klīṃ* to the Pin (*kīlaka*), salutation; 4 [the syllables] for the Application (*viniyoga*) on the feet and the heart—one should thus perform the placement (*nyāsa*).
In the skin—4 hrīṃ yaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ;
in the blood—4 hrīṃ raṃ hrīṃ namaḥ;
in the flesh—4 hrīṃ laṃ hrīṃ namaḥ.
In the fat—4 hrīṃ vaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ;
in the bone—4 hrīṃ śaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ;
in the marrow—4 hrīṃ ṣaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ.

In the *śukla* [kalā]: having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) with "4 hrīṃ saṃ hrīṃ namaḥ," [one recites] "oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ śrīmahātripurasundarī hrīṃ aiṃ sarvajñāyai hrāṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ."

7 Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ Śrī Mahātripurasundarī hrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the eternally contented one (nityatṛptāyai) with the two index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ). 7 Ka e ī la hrīṃ Mahātripurasundarī hrīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to the beginningless enlightened one (anādibodhāyai) with the two middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ).
7 Ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ Mahātripurasundarī hrīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to the independent Śiva (śivasvatantrāyai) with the two ring fingers (anāmikābhyāṃ).
7 *sakala* hrīṃ śrīmahātripurasundarī hrīṃ klīṃ nityamaluptāyai hrauṃ; to the two little fingers, *namaḥ*.
7 *sauḥ* aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīmahātripurasundarī hrīṃ aiṃ anantāyai hraḥ; to the palms and backs of the hands, *namaḥ*.
Thus are the six limbs, beginning with the heart. As for the visualization:
[one should visualize] the Tārikā, whose hands touch the forehead of one who is smeared with saffron and adorned with jasmine flowers.
In the rite of recitation (*japa*), one should meditate upon Ambikā, who has a gentle smile and gaze, who holds a bow, arrows, noose, and goad,
who deludes all people, who is adorned with red garlands and garments,
and who is as radiant as the *japā* flower.

Obeisance to you, O sole Mother of the World, who have four arms, are adorned with a crescent moon, possess high and beautiful breasts, are crimson with the hue of saffron, and hold in your hands a lotus, sugarcane, a noose, a goad, and flower-arrows.
Having meditated thus, [he forms] the Saṃkṣobhiṇī and other mudrās:
"4 Drāṃ, I display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā; 4 Drīṃ, I display the Sarvavidrāviṇī mudrā."
4 klīṃ, I display the Sarvākarṣaṇī mudrā; 4 blūṃ, I display the Sarvavaśaṅkarī mudrā;
4 saḥ, [I display] the Sarvonmādinī mudrā.
4 kroṃ, I display the seal of the Great Goad of All;
4 hskhphreṃ, I display the seal of the Sky-Traveler of All; 4 hsauḥ, I display the seal of the Seed-Syllable of All.
4 Aiṃ, I display the Sarvayonimudrā; 4 Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, I display the Sarvatrikhaṇḍāmudrā;
Kroṃ Hrīṃ, I display the Aṅkuśamudrā for Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, whose essence is aversion (dveṣa).
Hrīṃ! To Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, whose nature is passion (rāga), I display the noose mudrā (pāśamudrā).
Drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ śāṃ! To Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, whose nature consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, I display the flower-arrow mudrā (puṣpabāṇamudrā).
With the syllables *yaṃ* and *dhaṃ*, which are of the nature of the Self, I display the *ikṣucāpa* (sugarcane-bow) mudrā to Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī;
I display the *kirīṭa* (crown) mudrā;
I display the *makarakuṇḍala* (crocodile-earring) mudrā. Having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [I realize]: "All is Brahman; I am indeed Brahman."

"I am the Brahman-swan; I am that Śiva. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), "Having recited the root mantra according to my capacity, I shall perform the conclusion of the recitation," and having again performed the *sūryādinyāsa* and the *karāṅganyāsa*, and having meditated and displayed the mudrās, [he says]:
"Oṃ! You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by me."
O Goddess, may accomplishment be mine, abiding in you through your grace.
Having thus offered the *japa* into the left hand of the Goddess, one should recite the mantra of Annapūrṇā ten times for every hundred thousand recitations as its ancillary (*aṅga*).

Regarding this Śrī Siddhavidyā Annapūrṇeśvarī mantra: Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Yaṣṭik metre is the meter (*chanda*), the deity is Annapūrṇeśvarī, *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *śrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *klīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation for the sake of attaining the grace of Annapūrṇeśvarī.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ṛṣi* and so forth, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) of the hands beginning with *hrām*.
The wise man should meditate upon the Goddess, the Perfected Knowledge (*siddhavidyā*), in the great ocean of milk,
within a world resplendent with golden ramparts shining upon an island of jewels.
In a place enriched by the splendor of wish-fulfilling trees and provided with a lion throne,
she possesses the radiance of a thousand rising suns and blazes with various garments.
Devoted to bestowing the mantra of the Moon-crested One, adorned with jewels,
and exalted by the weight of her breasts which were shaped like golden jars.

Having meditated thus upon the Supreme Goddess— who possesses two arms and is filled with the bliss of Rudra’s *tāṇḍava* dance— and having displayed the *darvī* and *sruva* gestures, performed mental worship, and recited: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ namo bhagavati māheśvari annapūrṇe svāhā*, one should offer the recitation (*japa*) and contemplate the non-difference between the deities of the *cakra*, the Guru, and oneself.
Having reflected according to one's capacity, "I am Brahman," one should recite the morning hymn of the Goddess:
"O Mother, I bow to the lotus feet of the progenitor of the worlds;
salutations to Tripurasundarī, who is worshipped by Śiva and the other gods."
In the morning, I bow to the lotus feet of Tripurasundarī,
by whom Hari, Hara, and Viriñci perform the acts of creation and the rest.
In the morning, I bow to the lotus feet of Tripurasundarī,
the water used for washing whose feet shines as the Gaṅgā upon the head of Maheśvara.
In the morning, I bow to the illustrious Tripurasundarī, who resembles the rising sun and holds a noose, a goad, an arrow, and a bow in her hands.
In the morning, I bow to the lotus-feet of Tripurasundarī, by which this world shines and by whose grace it ceases [to appear as such].
To that man who recites these five verses daily at dawn,
the illustrious Tripurasundarī shall grant her own abode.
O Supreme Mistress, whose nature is the consciousness of the three worlds, O Śrīnātha’s eternal consort, by Your very command,
having risen at dawn for the sake of Your pleasure, I shall continue to follow the course of worldly existence.
O Supreme Goddess, O Śrī Tripurā, as I follow the journey of saṃsāra according to Your command,
may rivalry, contempt, strife, and negligence never overcome me, O Mother.
I know the proceeding of Dharma, and I know the cessation of Dharma;
O Sovereign of All, whether You abide within my heart or otherwise, I shall do exactly as I am directed by You.
Thus ends the morning recitation and praise of the Goddess.

Then, having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *haṃsa* mantra, one should perform the *ajapā-japa*—which consists of inhalation and exhalation, uttered throughout the preceding day and the subsequent day and night, numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred times—with the thought: "I am *Haṃsa*, I am *So'haṃ*, I am Śiva."

"I offer this according to their respective portions to the deities residing in the seven wheels. Having thus offered, I offer the recitation (japa) numbering six hundred to Gaṇapati residing in the Mūlādhāra; I offer the recitation numbering six thousand to Brahmā residing in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
I offer the recitation numbering six thousand to Viṣṇu residing in the Maṇipūra; [I offer] the recitation numbering six thousand to Rudra residing in the Anāhata.
I offer this: I offer one thousand recitations to the Jīva residing in the Viśuddha-cakra; I offer one thousand recitations to the Paramātman residing in the Ājñā-cakra;

I offer one thousand recitations to the Guru residing in the Brahmarandhra. Having thus offered, I shall perform the Ajapā-japa consisting of twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations uttered throughout the day and night. Thus.
Having performed the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*):

"Of this glorious Ajapā Mahāmantra, *haṃ* is the Ṛṣi; the unmanifest Gāyatrī is the metre (*chandas*); the venerable Paramahaṃsa is the deity (*devatā*); *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *saḥ* is the power (*śakti*); *so'haṃ* is the bolt (*kīlaka*); my application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the sake of liberation."

Then, having assigned the Ṛṣis and so forth to their respective locations in due order, one performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the hands using the seed-syllable of the six long vowels.
The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[One should meditate on the deity] who abides in coming and going, yet is devoid of movement and the like; who is the form of the lamp of consciousness, and the destroyer of darkness.
I behold you standing upon all people; I bow to the Swan, whose nature is the Supreme Self.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), one should mutter the *Haṃsa-gāyatrī* twenty-five times: "We know Haṃsa; we meditate upon Paramahaṃsa; may that Haṃsa inspire us. Then one should offer the recitation (*japa*) as follows:
To Gaṇapati, who resides there in the four-petalled lotus at the *mūlādhāra*, endowed with the syllables *vaṃ*, *śaṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, and *saṃ*.

I offer here the worship with the five services of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings to the one joined with the Śākinī-śakti. I offer to Gaṇapati, who is joined with the Śākinī-śakti, this recitation numbering six hundred times.
To Brahmā, who resides there in the six-petalled lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna, endowed with the syllables *aṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ*...
To Brahmā, who is joined with the power (śakti) Kākinī, here is fragrance... [offering]. Six thousand recitations have been performed for you; may they be equalized.
In Maṇipūra, in the ten-petalled lotus, accompanied by the ten syllables beginning with "Ḍaṃ" (Ḍa-Ṇa), to Viṣṇu residing there, who is joined with the power Lākinī, here is fragrance...
[offering]. Six thousand recitations have been performed for Viṣṇu; may they be equalized for you.
In the unstruck (*anāhata*) twelve-petaled lotus, which is endowed with the twelve syllables beginning with *ka* (12), to Rudra residing there, joined with the Śakti Śākinī, here [is] fragrance.
To Rudra, six thousand recitations are offered to you.
In the Viśuddhi [cakra], the sixteen-petaled lotus, which is endowed with the sixteen syllables beginning with *aṃ* (16), to Jīva residing there, joined with the Śakti Ḍākinī, here [is] fragrance.

To Jīva, one thousand recitations; to you, obeisance. To the Supreme Self (Paramātman) residing there within the two-petaled lotus of the Command (ājñā), joined with the syllables *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*, accompanied by the power Hākinī, [offer] here perfume... To the Supreme Self, one thousand recitations; to you, obeisance.

In the *brahmarandhra*, within the thousand-petaled lotus endowed with the infinite letters of the Mātṛkā, to the Guru stationed there, accompanied by the Śakti Yākinī, [offer] here perfume (*gandha*). "To the Guru, I offer one thousand recitations; to you, I offer [this]. Having thus offered, [recite] six hundred for Gaṇeśa, six thousand for Prajāpati, and six thousand for Gadāpāṇi.
One thousand [recitations] are offered to Pinākin; one thousand to the Liṅga of the Self; one thousand to the Supreme Self;
and one thousand indeed as an offering of Ajapās to the Guru.
There has never been,
nor will there ever be, a lore like this, a recitation like this, or a mantra like this.
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows liberation upon yogis;
by the mere mental resolve toward it, a person attains union [with the Divine].
Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*), the father should offer his own duties to the Goddess:
"Salutations to the Guru, who is present everywhere—whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing—and whose form is that of the Guru; salutations to the instrument."
O Goddess whose garment is the ocean, adorned with mountains for breasts, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.
Having thus petitioned the Earth, one should go outside the house, following one's breath and preceded by that [Earth’s] foot.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Morning Ritual," in the *Svacchandapaddhati* composed by Cidānandanātha, the disciple of the venerable Vimalānanda Bhagavat, who was devoted to the eightfold yoga beginning with Yama and Niyama.
Vibration. || 1 ||

Then, having performed the evacuation of waste and the purification and sipping of water according to the path taught in the Smṛtis, one should pray to the Vanaspati for the purpose of cleansing the teeth:
"May [this grant] long life, strength, fame, speech, progeny, cattle, and wealth."
O Lord of the Forest, grant us Brahmanic wisdom and mental acuity.
Having thus prayed and taken a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha) measuring twelve finger-breadths, one should say:
"For the destruction of foul odors from the mouth, for the purification of the teeth,
and for the spitting [of impurities], I perform the cleansing of my teeth."

Having cleansed his teeth with the mantra: *Oṃ klīṃ, to Kāmadeva, beloved by all people, blaze, blaze, burn brightly, bring all people under my control, svāhā*, and having washed his face with the root-vidyā, he should go to a sacred bathing place or similar location for the purpose of bathing. Having sprinkled the bank with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) and placed his garments and other items there, he should perform three rounds of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the root-mantra and enter the water up to his chest.
One should pray to the King of Tīrthas:
"You are the king of all tīrthas; you alone are the father of the worlds.
Grant me the requested tīrtha for the sake of liberation from all sins."
Thus it should be prayed:
"O you with sharp fangs and a massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, homage to you, Bhairava; you should deign to grant me your permission."

Having thus received the permission of Bhairava and performed the Vedic bath, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Deity, I shall perform the Tantric bath. Then [one should remember]:
"O Sun, those holy places on earth that have been touched by the rays of your light..."
By that truth, O God, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.

Having invoked the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* to be described hereafter, and having caused a shower of nectar to fall from the lunar orb of consciousness by means of the *Amṛteśvarī-Śrīvidyā*,
one should invoke [the rivers] Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī.
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in these waters.

Having established [the deity] with the *sannidhāpana-mudrā*, veiled it with the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā* while uttering "huṃ," protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and the wheel-gesture (*cakramudrā*), and having visualized the *Śrīcakra* there, one meditates upon the Goddess in its center. Then, with the root-mantra, one bathes the Goddess with that nectar using the *kalaśa-mudrā*. Regarding the red-colored sacred water (*tīrtha*) flowing from her lotus feet as the root-mantra, [one proceeds].

Having consecrated [the water] ten times while recollecting the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should immerse oneself and emerge three times in that sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). Then, forming the *yonimudrā* and placing three handfuls of water upon the head while uttering the first *kūṭa*, one says:

"By means of the *ātmatattva*, I purify the gross body, svāhā! Having uttered the second *kūṭa*, one says: "By means of the *vidyātattva*, I purify the subtle body, svāhā! Having uttered the third *kūṭa*, one says: "By means of the *śivatattva*, I purify the causal body."

Svāhā! Having washed both hands with the essence of all reality (*sarvatattva*), one should perform the libation as part of the bath: "To the gods, svāhā; I offer libation. To the sages, namaḥ; I offer libation. To the ancestors, svadhā; I offer libation. To all beings, vaṣaṭ;

I offer libation. May all the Bhairavas be satisfied. May all the Kṣetrapālas be satisfied. Having thus offered libations at the end of the root mantra with the words, "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, I offer libation," [one should proceed].
Having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) as before, one should dismiss that [deity] with the *niryāṇa-mudrā* and pay homage with the *yoni-mudrā*; this is the general procedure for bathing.

Now follows the specific procedure for bathing those who have been consecrated by the masters of the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣikta*). There are two types of bathing methods, distinguished as external and internal.
(p. 18) Today, during this interval, I shall respectfully tell you even a secret, which you should maintain both when you have attained the state of a noble person and otherwise.

Having recollected the *sa-ri-tra* mantra, one should contemplate from within the midst of its three syllables a flowing stream of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*) that is the object of meditative realization.
For yogins, the means to liberation for persons is through mere remembrance;
therefore, one should contemplate oneself as being bathed by that [remembrance] for the sake of the pacification of existence.
Then one should meditate upon the triad of rivers arising from the power of vibration and non-vibration:
another river is the carrier of bliss, and another is the river whose nature is pure consciousness.
In the center is another, whose nature is truth, consisting solely of consciousness and bliss;
she is composed of supreme bliss and is indeed the very essence of the Supreme Brahman.
Having reached the left side of the lotus, that river which flows to the end of the left foot is known as Bodharūpā, whose essential nature is that of the primordial Śakti.
That river, which flows at her right side and touches [her feet], is known by the name Saritsatyarūpā; she is the very embodiment of Ādiśambhu.
Having reached the center of the lotus, she flows through the space of the Suṣumṇā;
the Iḍā is renowned as the Gaṅgā river, and the Piṅgalā as the Yamunā river.
In the center, Sarasvatī is proclaimed; it is remembered as Prayāga.
Furthermore, the external bath is fivefold and consists of the nature of the five elements.
Since the fruit of all ablutions is obtained when the mantra-bath has been performed,
the seed-syllables of the five elements are said to be *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*.
Having consecrated the water held in his right hand with those [syllables] accompanied by the *bindu*,
he should sprinkle it three times upon his head using the application of the six fingers of his left hand.
First, one should draw in through the left nostril the remaining water consisting of light,
and then, having first washed away the impurities within, exhale it through the right nostril.
Having recited the Virecya mantra, one should throw it upon the stone;
for this Aghamarṣaṇa is the purifier of all sins.

Thus concludes the specific procedure for bathing. Having bathed in this manner and reached the bank, one should put on washed garments consecrated with the root mantra (*mūla*), recite the root mantra seven times, and then perform the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*) with [the mantra]:
"O you with upward-pointing hair, O three-eyed one, eater of flesh and blood!"
"Stay, O Goddess, in the binding of the topknot; O Cāmuṇḍā, O Unconquered One!"
Having tied the topknot with this mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā*,
and having applied a tilaka with sacred ash (vibhūti) and other substances,
[one should know that] for this Śrī Vibhūtidhāraṇa-mantra, Pippalāda is the seer (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda).

Rudra is the deity; the application is for the smearing with sacred ash (bhasma). Having taken the sacred ash in the left hand and prepared it with the right hand, [one recites]: "Oṃ, to Jātavedas... (Ṛg Veda 1.50.1). "Fire is ash, water is ash, earth is ash, air is ash, space is ash;
time, the directions, the mind, the eyes—everything here is ash. The triple longevity of Jamadagni, the triple longevity of Kasyapa... (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.37).

May he grant a hundred-year lifespan and a lifespan of strength. *Oṃ mānastoke tanaye*. *Oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ*. *Oṃ haruṃ jūṃ saḥ*. *Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe*. *Svaḥ vaḥ rbhubhūḥ*. *Oṃ saḥ jūṃ hauṃ oṃ*. *Oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi*. *Vāmadevāya namaḥ*. *Aghorebhyo*. *Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe*. *Īśāna saḥ*. *Ṛtana*. *Satyaṃ paraṃ brahma*. Thus.

Having consecrated [the ashes] with the twelve Vedic mantras, having sprinkled them while reciting "Oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ," and having rubbed them in while reciting "Viśvaṃ bhūtaṃ bhuvanam," one should circumambulate the head with the thumb and, saying "Salutation to the radiant Caṇḍa," draw a line in the middle of the forehead; then, using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the index finger, one applies the *tripuṇḍra*.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
If it is circular, there will be disease; if long, there is the destruction of austerity.
One should apply the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) obliquely with a measurement of six finger-breadths.
In the root-vidyā, at the head: 1.
At the forehead: *Aiṃ vada 2 vāgvādini aiṃ klinne kledini kledaya 2 mahākṣobhaṃ kuru 2 klīṃ sauḥ mokṣaṃ kuru 2 sauḥ shauṃ hsauṃ dīpinyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Jvālāmālinī, O Goddess, O Queen, you who bring about the destruction of all beings, O Jātavedasī! Blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up!
Huṃ huṃ huṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is for] the throat. Oṃ hrī uṃ! Arise, O Puruṣī! Why do you sleep? A danger has arisen; whether it be possible or impossible, tell me that, O Blessed One.
śamaya 2 svāhā | oṃ hrīṃ vahnivāsinyai namaḥ at the heart. oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce svāhā at the navel.
Oṃ srūṃ sahasrārāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—[recite] at the roots of the thighs.
Oṃ ślīṃ paśu hūṃ phaṭ—[recite] at the knees.
Oṃ hrīṃ sphura 2 prasphura 2 ghora ghoratara tanurūpa caṭa 2 pracaṭa 2 kaha 2 bama 2 bandhaya 2—[recite].
*Ghātaya 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā*— at the two ankles.
*Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṣrauṃ śrīṃ oṃ [ugraṃ vīraṃ mahāviṣṇuṃ jvalantaṃ sarvato mukham |] nṛsiṃhabhīṣaṇaṃ bhadraṃ mṛtyumṛtyuṃ namāmyaham*— at the feet.

*Kṣrauṃ oṃ namo bhagavate nṛsiṃhāya jvālāmāline dīptadaṃṣṭrāyāgninetrāya sarvarakṣoghnāya sarvabhūtavināśanāya sarvajvaravināśanāya daha 2 paca 2 rakṣa 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā*— at the two elbows. *Oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣa haritapiṅgalalohitākṣa dehi me dadāpaya svāhā*— at the two wrists.

Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Great Śarabha; oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ, obeisance to Śivā, the Great Śarabhī; obeisance for the pacification of obstacles on all limbs. Aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ, from the letter *ka* to the letter *kṣa*.
One should apply [the ash] with the *mātṛkā* at all the joints.

Having thus performed the application of the *vibhūti*, and having performed the Vedic *sandhyā*, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Deity, I shall perform the Tantric *sandhyā*. Then, preceded by the salutation to the Guru and others, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having meditated upon oneself in the form of the Goddess preceded by the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣis and others, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before, one takes water in the right hand and,

consecrating it with the root mantra using the *tattvamudrā* with the left hand, holds that water in the left hand and sprinkles it over the feet, heart, between the eyebrows, and all the limbs with the root mantra used both individually and collectively. Then, taking water again in the right hand, one brings it near the nose.

Having drawn [the breath] through the *iḍā* until the end, one should expel the black-colored water—purified by the washing away of all impurities—through the *piṅgalā*. Then, having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* by striking it with the *astra-mantra* upon a blazing diamond-stone in the left [channel], one should wash both hands and perform *ācamana*. Again, taking water in the right hand, consecrating it three times with the root mantra, drinking that water, and performing *ācamana* as before, one should take water in the left hand with the root mantra.
Having consecrated it once with mantras and sprinkled it as before,
[one should meditate on] the Sun, surrounded by the nine planets, attended by the twelve radiant zodiac signs,
holding a pair of lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons, and dispelling all darkness.
Having meditated thus:
*Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, salutation to Mārtaṇḍabhairava accompanied by the Śakti Prakāśā, to the Sun who is the soul of the twelve digits; this is your *arghya*, svāhā!*

Having meditated upon the Goddess within the solar disc, one offers the threefold *arghya* with the mantra: "O Mahātripurasundarī, who dwells in the center of the solar disc, this is your *arghya*, svāhā! Then [one praises her]: "She who wears the crescent moon shimmering upon her crown of radiant jewels..."
Having the luster of freshly smelted gold, she has the form of the solar disc.
Then, while recollecting [the deity] holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting,
the mantra-practitioner should mutter the auspicious Gāyatrī, which consists of three parts and has the nature of seed-syllables.
Having meditated: *Aiṃ vāgeśvarī ca vidmahe, klīṃ kāmeśvarī dhīmahi, sauḥ tannaḥ śaktiḥ pracodayāt*.

With water in hand, saying "Salutation to the Unbroken Circle" (*akhaṇḍamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*), one should circumambulate clockwise, visualize the Śrīcakra in the water, satisfy it nine times with the root mantra, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and then recite the Tripurā-gāyatrī as many times as possible, followed by the recitation of the Śrīvidyā. There is a specific rule regarding the three junctions of the day (*sandhyā*).

Therein, for the sake of accomplishing dharma, kama, and artha, one should perform the morning *saṃdhyā*. Having meditated upon the seed-syllable *hlāṃ*, yellow in luster, within a lotus at the *mūlādhāra* joined with the letters from *va* to *sa*, one should visualize the Fire situated within the nostrils as it issues forth into that lotus; therein one should contemplate Jyeṣṭhā, who is yellow-hued, three-eyed, four-armed, and who holds in her hands the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, a skull-bowl, and a serpent, resembling the rising sun.
Having meditated upon this mantra, one should recite it:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsbreṃ hsauṃ hlāṃ hsauṃ hrīṃ jyeṣṭhā sandhyāyai hlāṃ hsauṃ hlāṃ anuttaravarā śrīpādukāṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*.
With the *arghyamanu* mantra, one should offer the *arghya* libation three times to the Sun;
thereafter, in due order, one should satisfy Maṅgala, Carcika, Yoga, Harasiddha, and Hāṭaka, as well as those beginning with Aśita.
One who is composed should [worship] Kālakāla, Kālarātri, Bhīṣaṇa, and the eight Bhairavas,
using either water, corpses, or other ritual means.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsauṃ Amaṅgalanātha, Aṃ Asitāṅgabhairavānandanātha [5], Āṃ Maṅgalāmbā, Āṃ Brahmāṇī Parāmbā Śrī [5], Iṃ Carcikānātha, Iṃ Rurubhairavānandanātha [5], Iṃ Carcikāmbā, Iṃ Māheśvarī Parāmbā. [From this point onward, pages 14–17 of this manuscript are missing.]
I propitiate the venerable sandals, obeisance!
(5 times) *uṃ* Yogīśanātha *uṃ* Caṇḍabhairavānandanātha (5 times) *ūṃ* Yogīśāmbā *ūṃ* Kaumārī Parāmbā;
I propitiate the venerable sandals, obeisance!

5 Ṛṃ Hara Siddhanātha, Ṛṃ Krodhabhairavānandanātha; 5 Ṝṃ Harasiddhāmbā, Ṝṃ Vaiṣṇavīparāmbā, I propitiate the Śrīpādukā, obeisance! 5 Ḷṃ Hāṭakanātha, Ḷṃ Unmattabhairavānandanātha; 5 Ḹṃ Hāṭakāmbā, Ḹṃ Vārāhīparāmbā.
I satiate the venerable sandals; obeisance.
(5 times) EṂ Kālikālanātha, EṂ Kapālībhairavānandanātha. (5 times) AUṂ Kālikālāmbā, AIṂ Indrāṇī Parāmbā, I satiate the venerable sandals; obeisance.

5 Oṃ Kālarātrīnātha, Oṃ Bhīṣaṇabhairavānandanātha. 5 Oṃ Kālarātryambā, Oṃ Cāmuṇḍā Parāmbā, I satiate the venerable sandals; obeisance. 5 Aṃ Bhīṣaṇanātha, Aṃ Saṃhārabhairavanātha. 5 Aḥ Bhīṣaṇāmbā, Aḥ Mahālakṣmī Parāmbā.
Having performed the libation with "I satiate the Śrīpādukā, obeisance," one should stand facing the sun and recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times.
For one who is devoted to the Gāyatrī, knowledge arises after a long time.
We know the six-faced one; we meditate upon the one with variegated feet; may Śambhu impel us toward that.
One should then join that Goddess and her mantra within the radiance of the root [mantra], as it was previously prepared in the center of the solar disc.
Having performed the worship with the thousand-syllable *prastāra*, one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*.

One should contemplate the Root Mantra from the base (*mūlādhāra*) up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), as having the splendor of the rising sun and being the very nature of eternal bliss. (1)
One should meditate upon the Vāgbhava syllable at the root-lotus, beautiful with peaks like lightning and gold;
and upon the Great Manmatha at the twelve-petaled lotus, which resembles the sun.
In the thousand-petalled lotus, which is like a swan, a lotus, and the stainless smile of the autumn moon,
and within the hollow of the pedestal whose color is that of the crimson ocean, resides the supreme fourth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) accompanied by Śakti.

Having meditated thus, and having first performed the visualization of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-dhyāna*), one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) three times.

Then, having visualized the venerable Supreme Deity who resides in that [seat], worshipped Her with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), and displayed the ritual gestures (*mudrā*), one should recite the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) as many times as possible.
Having offered the recitation preceded by the visualization of the seer and the six-limbed yoga, one should join the palms in reverence and utter the root-mantra.

Oṃ, salutations to Tripurasundarī, the auspicious one, the well-pleased, the easily accessible, she whose face is like the moon, who is worshipped by gods and demons, whose lotus-feet are as red as the *japā* flower, served by hosts of *yoginīs*, whose mind is elevated by the intoxication of honey, whose garment and seat are the twilight, she who is eternally exultant in great bliss,
ruddy with the rays of rubies, whose nature is *bindu* and *nāda*, whose nature is pure consciousness alone: *hsaiṃ hsrīṃ hsauṃ shauṃ srhīṃ srhauḥ*.

Sa ha ka e ī la hrīṃ | Sa ha ka e ī la hrīṃ | Sa ha ka e ī la hrīṃ | Namo devi āgaccha āgaccha | Sāṃnidhyaṃ kuru kuru | Sarvato māṃ rakṣa rakṣa | Vaha vaha | Ānandaya ānandaya | Modaya modaya | Sthāpaya sthāpaya | Prāpaya prāpaya | Sarvakāryāṇi manasā sādhaya sādhaya | Poṣaya poṣaya | Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ.

Hsraiṃ hsrīṃ hsrauṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sa ha e ī la hrīṃ sa ha e ka e ī la hrīṃ ha sa ka e ī la hrīṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, O You whose form is the Blessed One, whose form is auspiciousness, O Destroyer of Sin! Bring the king under my control, bring him! Shatter misfortune, shatter it! Attract women, attract them! Saturate them, saturate them! Agitate their minds, agitate them! Delude them, delude them!

Make it shine, make it shine! Bestow upon me good fortune, bestow it! Produce in me beauty, produce it! *hsraṃ hsrīṃ hsrauṃḥ* *ka e ī la hrīṃ* *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ* *sakala hrīṃ namaḥ*. O you who bring about auspiciousness, whose body is resplendent with the luster of jeweled ornaments, seated upon a red lotus, holding a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows in your four arms.

O Candraśekhara, O Four-Armed One, O Bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life, O Divine One whose divine body is adorned with celestial garlands, accomplish, accomplish all my desires; expand, expand them; make them firm, make them firm! *ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ hsrīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ hasakahalahrauṃ hasakahalahrīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ*. Salutations to you, the Giver of Boons, O Retas, O Suretas, O Truth, O Eternal, O Stainless One!

O you who cause the agitation of the world, O lotus-like one who bestows liberation, O you of lovely limbs, O Kamalavatī, O you who abide on the southern path: grant a kingdom, grant it! Spread fame, spread it! Paralyze the army, paralyze it! Split it, split it! Crush it, crush it! Cut it, cut it! Eradicate it, eradicate it! Hasaka halahrīṃ hasaka halahrīṃ sahaka halahrīṃ hasakalahrīṃ sakalahrīṃ namaḥ.

O Supreme Goddess, whose nature is the Supreme Self, showering the nectar of compassion! *Drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*! O enchanting one, abode of auspiciousness, variegated with the rays of rubies, whose limbs are tender as the unbroken Kuṇḍalinī! Draw me toward you with your goad, draw me toward you! Enthrall me with your noose, enthrall me! Pierce me with your arrow, pierce me! *Hasakalaraḍāṃ hasakalaraḍīṃ hasakalaraḍauṃ hasakalaraḍaiṃ sahakalaraḍīṃ*.

*Hasakalaraḍauṃḥ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *sahasakalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*, obeisance to Tripurā! Carry [us], carry [us]! Cause [the drums] to sound, cause [them] to sound! O Queen of Tripura, Sovereign of Wisdom, praised by heroes, fanned with chowries by the Vidyādharas, gladden us, gladden us! O Full-eyed One, O Three-eyed One, O Tripurasundarī! *Hasakalaraḍrāṃ*, *hasakalaraḍrīṃ*, *hasakalaraḍrauṃḥ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*.
Salutations to you, O dweller of the three cities, O Goddess who is the refuge of the three cities! I take refuge in you; I take refuge well; I take refuge completely; I always take refuge.

I take refuge in you, O compassionate one, O protector, O you who are affectionate toward those who have come for shelter! O Madana, O you whose body is Madana, O you who captivate the hearts of all people, O you who enter the hearts of all beings, O you who bring all creatures under control! Bring all beings under my control! Fulfill, fulfill my desires! Grant me fame!
Cause [them] to be given; destroy, destroy the afflictions! Destroy, destroy the enemies! Tear asunder, tear asunder! Bind, bind! Cut, cut! Grant liberation, grant liberation!
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hasakalaraḍarahaiṃ Hasakalaraḍahauṃḥ Hasakalaraḍahauḥ Sahakalahrīṃ Sahakalahrīṃ Sahasakalahrīṃ.
Oṃ, homage to you, O Lalitā, whose form is beauty, O intoxicating-eyed one, O you of great form, O formless one, O multiformed one!

O you of beautiful form, most enchanting, in the form of a woman, O you who bring women and men under your control, grant me happiness, grant me a wife, bring her hither, bring her! Reveal the treasure, reveal it! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hasakalaraḍarasahaiṃ Hasakalaraḍarasahīṃ Hasakalaraḍarasahauṃḥ Hasakalahrīṃ Sakalahrīṃ Sakalahrīṃ Ramalini, O fulfiller of the desired object, O knower of the mind!

O You who are worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Sadāśiva; O One worthy of worship, fulfill, fulfill my heart's desires! Deliver me from the ocean, deliver me! Shatter, shatter misfortune! Spread, spread throughout the boundaries! Cut down, cut down evil deeds! Destroy, destroy the magical spell (kṛtyā)! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hasakalaraḍarasaharaiṃ Hasakalaraḍarasaharauṃḥ!

Hasakalaraḍarasaharaumḥ, hasakalaraḍarasaharaim, hasakalaraḍarasaharīm, ka e ī lahrīṃ, hasakahalahrīṃ, sakalahrīṃ, aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, hsaiṃ hsklīṃ hsauṃḥ! O Tripurāsiddhi, O Tripurāmbāyogeśvarī, O you of the great form of Kula, O you of the great form of Aruṇāvarta, hasakṣamalavarayūṃ, hasakṣamalavarayīṃ, O you who bring all kings under control, O you who fulfill all prosperity!

O bestower of all sovereignty, remover of all suffering, giver of all happiness! *hasakalaraḍara saharaḍaiṃ*, *hasakalaraḍara saharaḍīṃ*, *hasakalaraḍarasaharaḍauḥ*, *hasakalaraḍarasaharaḍauḥ*, *hasakalaraḍarasaharaḍīṃ*, *hasakalaraḍarasaharaḍaiṃ*; *ka e ī la hrīṃ*, *hasakahalahrīṃ*, *sakalahrīṃ*, *ha 5 ka 4 sa 3*.

Obeisance, Svāhā, Hrīṃ, Aiṃ, Īṃ— to Mahāśrī Tripurā, who consists of all bliss, who resides in the wheel of the *bindu*, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, who is the Supreme Śakti, who embodies all knowledge, who is endowed with the *kalās* of Mahābhairavī, who is the soul of all things, and who is the essence of the wheel of the *bindu*.
May this thousand-syllable expansion (*prastāra*) be complete.
Thus ends the procedure for the morning twilight (prātaḥ-sandhyā).

Now, regarding the midday twilight (mādhyāhna-sandhyā): having meditated upon the seed-syllable *hlīṃ*, which is red in color, within a lotus marked by the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* on an unstruck (*anāhata*) drum, and having [the goddess] emitted as before, one should contemplate her standing in the center of the solar disc, multiform, with a red body, and in the full bloom of youth.
Visualizing her likewise holding a rosary and a book in her left [hand], and similarly in the north, one should recite this:
*Hrīṃ hsauṃ hrīṃ vāmāsandhyāyai hrīṃ hsau hrīṃ śrīpādukāṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*.
Having performed the libation as before, one should cause her to dissolve into her own place. This is the midday *saṃdhyā*.

Then, for the evening twilight (sandhyā): having meditated upon the seed-syllable *hrauṃ*, which is white in color, within a lotus situated either between the eyebrows or at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), joined with the two syllables *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*, or joined with the letters from *va* to *kṣa*; and having emitted [the deity] as before, [one should meditate on her] as being white in color, four-armed, and stationed in the center of the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*).
She bears the trident of fearlessness, as well as the skull and the raised index finger.
And having meditated upon the fierce Raudrī on the left side, who is aged, endowed with three eyes, and adorned with various ornaments, one should recite this mantra.

Hraum Hsauṃ Hraum, to Raudrī Sandhyā, hraum hsauṃ [five times], I satisfy the venerable sandals; obeisance. Having first performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in this manner, one should lead her into dissolution in her own place. Then, having joined that goddess and her mantra into the root radiance (*mūlatejas*), and having performed the worship as before, one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. Thus is the procedure for the three daily junctures (*sandhyātraya*).
He describes the specific meditation for the three junctions (sandhyās):
At the root-support (mūlādhāra), in the center of the yellow-colored circle of fire,
one should recite and meditate upon the Vāgbhava-kūṭa at dawn, which has the brilliance of lightning.
At midday, the practitioner of mantras should practice while meditating on the one called Kāmarāja in the heart, within the solar disc, possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns.

In the evening, while reciting the mantra with concentration, one should meditate upon the Śaktikūṭa within the lunar disc, located either between the eyebrows or at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Then, as an ancillary part of that [rite], having recited the *annapūrṇā-daśāṃśa* mantra and offered the recitation, he should then fetch water facing the current,

pay obeisance to the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and while reciting the *Jalahasta-stotra*, with speech restrained, looking only at his own feet, not touching or looking at other people, and not conversing with them, he should go to the main hall of worship (*pūjāgṛha*).

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Purification, Ritual Sipping, Bathing, and the Twilight Devotions," in the *Svacchandapaddhati* composed by the venerable Cidānandanātha. || 2 ||
Now, regarding the sacrificial vessel: whatever [vessel] is adorned with lac-dye, made beautiful with various patterns, and smeared with cow dung upon the ground;
Abounding with garlands of flowers shimmering above, perfumed by incense,
beautiful with rows of lamp circles, and radiant with scattered blossoms.
Having arrived there, the wise man, silent and devoted to meditation,
should worship the one who possesses all ornaments and who accepts the worship of Tripurā.

Salutation to the pavilion for the worship of Tripurā. There, having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square at the front of the threshold, and having placed upon it a copper vessel containing water along with its base (ādhāra), which has been washed with the Astra-mantra:
"Aiṃ, salutation to the support (ādhāra) which is the essence of the ten kalās of the fire-mandala that bestows dharma."
*Klīṃ*, salutation to the vessel which is the solar orb (*arka-maṇḍala*), the essence of the twelve rays that bestow wealth;
*Sauḥ*, salutation to the vessel-nectar which is the lunar orb (*soma-maṇḍala*), the essence of the sixteen rays that bestow desire.
Having cast perfume, flowers, and unbroken rice grains with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having displayed the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), [one sprinkles] with that water while reciting: *Sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*.

Having thus sprinkled the door with water, one should worship the deities of the door: "Oṃ, obeisance to the door of the sacrificial hall," [offering] above; "Oṃ dvāṃ, obeisance to Dvāraśrī," on the right branch of the door; "Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," and "Oṃ guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus";
on the left branch, "Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī," and "Oṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā"; and below, "Oṃ, obeisance to the threshold."
Having performed the worship of the door while recollecting the root mantra:
"May those spirits who are the enemies of heretics— those on the earth, those in the intermediate space,
and those situated in the heavenly world— be destroyed by the command of Śiva."
Striking with the heels of the feet and snapping the fingers, one should fill the ocean with vajras;
then, according to tradition, one should perform the three claps with sound.

Having entered the interior of the house by contracting the left limb and stepping forward with the right foot, and having sprinkled the pavilion and other areas with arghya water, one should worship Brahmā in the southwest direction with: "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of Vāstu. Then [one should worship him] with:
"O you of sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon!"
Salutations to you, O Bhairava; you should grant me permission.

(35) Thus, having obtained the permission of Bhairava, one should purify the place of recitation (*japasthāna*). Having inspected it with the Root-Mantra (*mūlavidyā*) and sprinkled it with the Weapon-Mantra (*astra*), one should then cover the door. Upon the altar (*vedikā*), having spread out either a tiger skin, *kuśa* grass, a red cloth, a variegated woolen blanket, or any other such material, one should sprinkle the seat with the Root-Mantra. There, one should draw the *Mātṛkā*-lotus, consisting of a pericarp, filaments, eight petals, and a square [enclosure].

Having consecrated the seat with the mantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti)," one should sit upon it in the svastika posture or other such manner, facing either east or north. Then, having placed the Śrīcakra—crafted from gold or other materials—upon a washed pedestal in front of oneself, [one should recite] at the end of the entire Vidyā of the circle of Yoginīs according to the sequence to be described therein.

Having uttered the *kūṭas* of Śakti, Kāma, and Vāgbhava, one should place a flower such as a pearl or a pearl-like gem; then, having set aside the perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth on one's right side, one should place a beautiful water-pot (*kumbha*) filled with highly fragrant water on the left.
Having placed lamps all around, one should perform another practice in front.

One should place the vessel behind for the washing of the hands. Then, with palms joined in *añjali*, one should bow to the lotus feet of one's own Guru by means of the *pādukā* mantra, within the center of the full moon disc situated in the middle of the interior of the white thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) upon one’s own head. On the left: *Oṃ guṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*. On the right: *Oṃ...* (p. 36).
Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. In front: Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Goddess (Śrīparadevatā). Oṃ sauḥ, to the Weapon (astra), Phaṭ!

Having thus performed the purification of the hands for the sake of self-protection, and having performed the binding of the ten directions with the triple *tāla* [clap] using the *sphoṭana-mudrā*, [one recites]: "Oṃ, protect, protect the three worlds, Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!"
Having thus visualized a rampart of fire surrounding oneself, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). It is as follows:

having meditated upon a four-petalled lotus with filaments, yellow in color, resting on the final letter of the fourth group (pa), four fingers wide and circular, located four fingers above the *mūlādhāra*;
and within its pericarp, a red-colored triangle composed of the moon, sun, and fire.

Having visualized [the self] facing oneself, one should contemplate within that [space] the drop (bindu) named Kāma, resembling the Japā and Bandhūka flowers, brilliant as ten million suns yet as cool as ten million moons, and pervaded by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Above that,

one should contemplate the Kuṇḍalinī energy, whose nature is consciousness, who is the embodiment of all vidyās, blazing with the splendor of ten million flashes of lightning, thinner than a lotus fiber, shaped like a sleeping serpent, and possessing three and a half coils.

Having meditated upon her as she remains [coiled], one should strike her with the staff of the syllable *huṃ* and, having raised her up by means of the upward-moving breath (*ūrdhvapavana*) according to the method taught by the Guru,

one should conquer that Kuṇḍalinī— by piercing the sequence of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) beginning from the *mūlādhāra*— within the variegated channel (*citranāḍī*) inside the *suṣumnā*, against the full moon consisting of the nature of the letter *va*, which resides in the center of the pericarp of the white thousand-petaled lotus at the head, facing downwards.
Then, having satiated Kuṇḍalinī— who consists of the letters— with a stream of nectar flowing from that [crown],

one should lead her back to the Mūlādhāra and establish her there in the same manner; she, whose nature is a flow of nectar, takes the form of the Akula-amṛta and, by means of the deities of the elements and letters within the Ādhāra situated inside the Suṣumnā, drenches them with "Svāhā" according to the sequence of creation through the six cakras beginning with Ājñā.

I salute you, the mother of Brahmā and Viṣṇu— the royal female swan sporting in the lotus-forest of the foundational support (Ādhāra), the celestial path traversing the great intermediate space within, the lightning of bliss for the enemy of Manmatha, and the consort of the Lord.
She is the great female serpent for the elephant of Ānanda-Valmīka, a swan sporting in the lake of the sky,
an unending streak of light from the jewel-lamp, and a stainless creeper that bestows [bliss] reaching up to Brahmā.
We behold the seal of bliss moving within the path— shining forth at the first departure, yet becoming nectar at the return.

Now, the practice of mantra-yoga: Having meditated upon the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* in the fire-maṇḍala at the *mūlādhāra*, shining like a flash of lightning, yellow in color, reaching as far as the *anāhata* with its crest of *nāda*; and having meditated upon the *kāmarāja-kūṭa* in the sun-maṇḍala at the *anāhata*, shining with the color of the rising sun, reaching as far as the *ājñā* with its crest of *nāda*; [one meditates] in the moon-maṇḍala at the *ājñā-cakra*.

Having meditated upon the Śakti-peak, which possesses a luster equal to the full moon, is known as the crest of Kāmarāja, reaches up to the lunar orb of consciousness within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and has the peak of sound (nāda) attained therein; one should then [meditate upon] the Full Vidyā consisting of three peaks, extending from the base to the aperture of Brahmā, as slender as a lotus fiber.
One should meditate upon her, radiant as the rising sun, for the pacification of inauspiciousness.

Having joined [the breath] with the syllable *so'ham*, I unite the earth element (*pṛthvītattva*), together with Brahmā, the Nivṛtti-kalā, the sense of smell, the organ of generation, and the quality of bliss, with the syllable *laṃ*.

Pervading from the feet up to the knees, I dissolve the earth element into the water element. With the syllable *vaṃ*, I unite the water element, together with Viṣṇu, the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā, the organ of speech, the organ of excretion, and the quality of passion, into fire. Pervading from the knees up to the navel, I dissolve the water element into fire.
I dissolve [the element]. I join the fire-principle (*tejastattva*), together with its Rudra-vidyā, eyes, form, feet, movement, and so forth, into the air.
Pervading from the navel up to the heart, I dissolve the fire-principle into the air.
I join the air-principle (*vāyutattva*), together with its Yama, Īśvara, peace, skin, touch, hands, grasping, and so forth, into space.

Pervading from the heart up to the space between the eyebrows, I dissolve the element of air (*vāyu-tattva*) into space (*ākāśa*). Hsauḥ! O Sadāśiva, I unite the element of space—accompanied by the sense of hearing, sound, speech, and the faculty of speaking, as well as the state beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*)—with the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*). Pervading from the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), I dissolve the element of space into the ego-principle. That ego-principle [I dissolve] into the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*), and that Great Principle into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
I dissolve that primordial nature into the Supreme Brahman. Having dissolved everything into the Paramātman by means of the mind through the process of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one [visualizes] that personified sin (pāpapuruṣa) with the murder of a Brahmin as its head and the theft of gold as its two arms.
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the teacher's bed.
The pair of feet associated with that [body] were the cause of the downfall of his limbs and minor members;
his body-hairs were minor transgressions, and his beard and eyes were red.
One should contemplate the evil within the belly as black in color, facing downwards, the size of a thumb, and holding a sword and shield in its hands.
Having meditated thus with these two and a half verses, one should consider [the body] dried up by the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, contemplate it as burnt by the seed-syllable *raṃ*,

cause a rain of nectar to fall by means of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, visualize a divine body produced by the seed-syllable *laṃ*, and contemplate consciousness by means of the seed-syllable *haṃ*; then, following the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), [one should place it] from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the throat, from the throat down to the heart, and from the heart down to the navel.

Pervading [the body] sequentially from the navel to the knees and from the knees to the feet with the syllables *haṃ*, *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *laṃ*, and *vaṃ*—which represent the five elements—one pervades [the body] from one's own head to the feet as consisting of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.

From the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*) arises; from primordial nature, the Great Principle (*mahat*); from the Great Principle, the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*); and from the ego-principle, the element of ether (*ākāśatattva*) is produced.

Hsauṃḥ! I generate the element of space (ākāśatattva), accompanied by Sadāśiva, the Śāntyatīta level, sound, speech, utterance, and so forth. I pervade it from the head down to the throat. Then, from space, I generate the element of air (vāyutattva). I generate the element of air, accompanied by Yama, Īśvara, the Śānti level, touch, the hands, grasping, and so forth. I pervade it from the throat down to the heart. Then, from air, I generate the element of fire (agnitattva). Raṃ.

Through the Rudra-vidyā, I generate the fire-element (tejas-tattva) together with the eyes, form, feet, movement, and so forth; I cause it to pervade from the heart to the navel. Then, from fire, I generate the water-element (ap-tattva); *Vaṃ*, the Viṣṇu-pratiṣṭhā, together with the tongue, taste, anus, excretion, and so forth—I generate that water-element; I cause it to pervade from the navel to the knees. Then, from water, I generate the earth-element (pṛthivī-tattva); *Laṃ*.

"I generate the earth-element (pṛthvītattva), accompanied by the bliss of the anus, genitals, and thighs, as well as the cessation of speech. I pervade [the body] from the knees down to the feet. Thus ends the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

Now follows the consecration of the constituent elements (dhātupratiṣṭhā). Therein, first, at the throat is the wheel (cakra) called Viśuddhi, consisting of the vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga.

One should install Ḍākinī there as before, within that [cakra] which is endowed with its own vowel, possesses sixteen petals, and is smoke-colored. In the heart, one should install Rākiṇī as before, within the cakra known as Anāhata, which is a twelve-petaled lotus accompanied by the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, and is smoke-colored. In the navel, [one should install Lākinī] within the cakra known as Maṇipūraka, which is a ten-petaled lotus accompanied by the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*.

In the center of that [lotus], one should install Lākinī as before, resembling a sapphire (*indranīla*). Upon the *liṅga* is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*-cakra, a six-petaled lotus accompanied by the syllables from *ba* to *la*, with the color of the rising sun; in its center, one should install Kākinī as before. At the *mūlādhāra* is a four-petaled lotus accompanied by the syllables from *va* to *sa*, red in color; in its center, [one should install] Śākinī as before.

One should install [the deities]. In the middle of the eyebrows, one should install Hākinī as before within the wheel called Ājñā, which is a two-petalled lotus endowed with the two syllables *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*, white in color. By means of the mantra *haṃsaḥ*, having brought the individual soul (*jīvātman*) from the presence of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) to the heart-lotus, one should install Kuṇḍalinī in the *mūlādhāra* as before. This is the installation of the elements (*dhātupratiṣṭhā*).

Now, the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths). Of this venerable *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *virāṭ* is the meter (*chandas*), the deity is Prāṇa-śakti, *āṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *kroṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the consecration of my vital breaths.
[Recite] "Hrīṃ yaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ" in the heart, and likewise on the skin and in the blood.
Hrīṃ raṃ hrīṃ namaḥ to the flesh; hrīṃ laṃ hrīṃ namaḥ to the fat;
hrīṃ vaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ to the bone.
Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) with *hrīṃ śaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* on the thumb (*sajjāyām*),

*hrīṃ ṣaṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* on the index finger (*śukle*), and *hrīṃ saṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* [on the middle finger], one should assign *yaṃ raṃ* to the thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhā*), *raṃ laṃ* to the index fingers (*tarjanī*), and *laṃ vaṃ* [to the middle fingers].

*Madhyamā*: VAṂ ŚAṂ Anāmikā; *Kaniṣṭhā*: ṢAṂ SAṂ Karatala. Thus are the six limbs, beginning with the heart. The visualization (*dhyāna*): One should meditate upon the Goddess, the power of vital breath (*prāṇa-śakti*), who is ruddy and clad in ruddy garments, wearing a ruddy crown and possessing ruddy sprout-like lips.
She has a pair of lotus-eyes as red as the dawn, a face with a beautiful smile,
and she holds a cluster of blossoms and a noose in her two hands.
Having meditated thus, one should display the mudrās:
Oṃ, the flower-cluster mudrā; Oṃ, the noose mudrā; Oṃ, the crown mudrā.
Oṃ, bestow the makarakuṇḍala-mudrā;
having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra) and touched the heart, [recite]:
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ! May the vital breaths (prāṇa) of this one [amuṣya] be here; may the life-force (jīva) of this one [amuṣya] be here.

"Remaining here, may all the senses of that person, or the speech, mind, and breath of that person, come here; may they remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Thus one should recite three times. Again, having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. This is the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Thus ends the purification of the ground (*bhūśuddhi*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and the consecration of the constituents (*dhātupratiṣṭhā*) in the *Svacchandapaddhati* composed by the venerable Cidānandanātha.
The third vibration, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Vitality" (Prāṇapratiṣṭhāvidhi). || 3 ||

Oṃ. Of this Śrī Mātṛkānyāsa, the Seer is Śabdārṣṭi, the Metre is Virāṭ, the Deity is Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī, the Seeds are the consonants, the Powers are the vowels, and the Bindus are the Nail. Its application is in the Nyāsa for the sake of attaining the grace of Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī and for the sake of attaining fitness for the practice of Śrīvidyā. [One should perform the assignment: "Salutation to the Seer" on the head; "Salutation to the Metre" on the mouth; "Salutation to the Deity" on the heart.

Salutation to the Seed-syllable (bīja) on the right breast; salutation to Power (śakti) on the left breast; salutation to the Pin (kīlaka) at the navel; salutation to the Application (viniyoga) on the feet.
Oṃ aṃ kaṃ oṃ āṃ [to] the thumbs; Oṃ iṃ caṃ oṃ īṃ [to] the index fingers.

Oṃ uṃ ṭaṃ oṃ ūṃ [to] the middle fingers; oṃ eṃ taṃ oṃ aiṃ [to] the ring fingers; oṃ oṃ paṃ oṃ auṃ [to] the little fingers; oṃ aṃ yaṃ oṃ aḥ [to] the palms. In this manner, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the heart and so forth, and then meditate.
Therein, having visualized upon one's own head the *mātṛkā* lotus consisting of a pericarp, filaments, eight petals, and a square, one should contemplate within its pericarp—

Hsauṃḥ! Outside of that, on the filaments, one should contemplate the vowels; on the eight petals, the eight groups of consonants beginning with *ka*; in the directions of the square, the letter *ṭa*; and in the intermediate directions, the letter *va*. In the center of that, one should meditate upon the Mātṛkā.
"O Great One, I indeed consider myself [united] with the divine form of the Mātṛkā; O Seed-syllable, reveal all the Tantras! Sahada Sahada!
Even one who meditates upon you with the mind but once—be it for a great length of time or for a moment—in that which is most worthy of honor, O Unmanifest, Pure Knowledge, is liberated.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with the five offerings, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*):
*aṃ namaḥ* on the palm of the right hand; *āṃ namaḥ* on the palm of the left hand.
Iṃ namaḥ on the back of the right hand;
īṃ namaḥ on the back of the left hand; uṃ namaḥ from the right elbow to the tips of the fingers.
Oṃ, salutation to [the deity] beginning from the left elbow. Having placed the remaining ten vowels starting from the right thumb and ending at the left thumb,

one should then place four letters each upon the four joints of the fingers, starting from the right index finger and ending at the left index finger, with the consonant groups beginning from *ka* and ending with *sa*.
One should place [the letters] on the thumbs and likewise on the tips of the fingers. This is the *bhūtalipimātṛkā-nyāsa*.

Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the inner *mātṛkā*: one should meditate upon the *mātṛkā* consisting of vowels, whose nature is the phonemes, which is composed of consciousness, and which has entered within the six *cakras*.

I bow to that Great Mother within, who shatters the fear of worldly existence; she is easily attained through the state of the pervasive and pervading mantra, whose essence is the awakening to Brahman, who consists of all the Vedas, who wears diverse garments, and who is radiant with the ornaments of rubies.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*). The Sūtra states (p.

46): "In the foundation, the *liṅga*, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, and the forehead; in the two-petaled, the sixteen-spoked, the twenty-two- and ten-petaled, the twelve-spoked, and the four-petaled [cakras]."

I bow to that which is at the end of the vowels (ha), in the midst of the consonants (kṣa), joined with the syllables ḍa, pha, ka, ṭha, and sa, located in the region of the throat, endowed with the meaning of the principles (tattvas), considered the body of all, and existing in the form of phonemes.

There, in the four petals of the *mūlādhāra*, one should assign [the syllables] starting from the east: *oṃ vaṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ śaṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ ṣaṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ saṃ namaḥ*. In the six petals of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*—
Oṃ baṃ namaḥ, oṃ bhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ maṃ namaḥ, oṃ yaṃ namaḥ, oṃ raṃ namaḥ, oṃ laṃ namaḥ; thus one should assign [these] starting from the east.
[These are] in the ten petals of the Maṇipūra at the navel.
Oṃ ḍaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ, oṃ taṃ namaḥ, oṃ thaṃ namaḥ, oṃ daṃ namaḥ,
oṃ dhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ naṃ namaḥ, oṃ paṃ namaḥ.
"Oṃ phaṃ namaḥ"—thus one should assign [the syllables] starting from the east.
In the heart, within the twelve petals of the Anāhata [cakra], [one assigns]:
"Oṃ kaṃ namaḥ," "Oṃ khaṃ namaḥ," "Oṃ gaṃ namaḥ."
Oṃ ghaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ, oṃ caṃ namaḥ, oṃ chaṃ namaḥ, oṃ jaṃ namaḥ,
oṃ jhaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ñaṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṭaṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ ṭhaṃ namaḥ; one should assign [the syllables] starting from the east with "Oṃ" and so forth.
In the throat, within the sixteen petals of the Viśuddha [cakra], [one assigns]:
Oṃ aṃ namaḥ, Oṃ āṃ namaḥ, Oṃ iṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ īṃ namaḥ, oṃ uṃ namaḥ, oṃ ūṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṛṃ namaḥ, oṃ ṝṃ namaḥ, oṃ ḷṃ namaḥ,
oṃ ḹṃ namaḥ, oṃ eṃ namaḥ, oṃ aiṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ oṃ namaḥ, oṃ auṃ namaḥ, oṃ aṃ namaḥ, oṃ aḥ namaḥ; thus one should assign [these] starting from the east.
[These are assigned] in the two-petalled Ājñā-cakra between the eyebrows.
Oṃ haṃ namaḥ, Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ—thus one should perform the placement. This concludes the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa. Now follows the external Mātṛkā-nyāsa. The visualization (dhyāna):
Her face, arms, waist, and chest are adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet; she wears a radiant crown bound with a crescent moon, and her full, lofty breasts are prominent.
With her lotus-like hands, she holds a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the goddess of learning (Vidyā).
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who bears the crescent moon, possesses radiant white luster, and has three eyes.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). The Sūtra states:
"One should place the vowels one by one on the forehead, the face, the surrounding [areas], the eyes, the ears, the nose, the two cheeks, the lips, the teeth, the head, and the tongue."
One should place four groups [of letters] on the roots, middles, joints, palms, and tips of the hands and feet; the fifth group should be placed on the sides and the back.
Having placed [the seeds] at the navel and the heart, one should place the pervasive [syllables] upon the ten locations:
*aṃ* namas on the forehead; *āṃ* namas on the circumference of the mouth; *iṃ* namas on the right eye; *īṃ* namas on the left eye; *uṃ* namas on the right ear; *ūṃ* namas on the left ear.

In the right nostril—*ṛṃ namaḥ*; in the left nostril—*ṝṃ namaḥ*; on the right cheek—*ḷṃ namaḥ*; on the left cheek—*ḹṃ namaḥ*; on the upper lip—*eṃ namaḥ*; on the lower lip—*aiṃ namaḥ*; on the upper teeth—*oṃ namaḥ*; on the lower teeth—*auṃ namaḥ*; on the crown of the head—*aṃ namaḥ*; on the tongue—*aḥ*.

*Namaḥ*; on the right shoulder—*kaṃ namaḥ*; on the right elbow—*khaṃ namaḥ*; on the right wrist—*gaṃ namaḥ*; at the base of the fingers of the right hand—*ghaṃ namaḥ*; on the tips of the fingers of the right hand—*ṅaṃ namaḥ*.
On the left shoulder: *caṃ* namaḥ; on the left elbow: *chaṃ* namaḥ;
on the left wrist: *jaṃ* namaḥ; at the base of the left fingers: *jhaṃ* namaḥ;
on the tips of the left fingers: *ñaṃ* namaḥ; at the base of the right thigh: *ṭaṃ* namaḥ.
At the right knee—Ṭhaṃ namaḥ; at the right ankle—Ḍaṃ namaḥ;
at the base of the toes of the right foot—Ḍhaṃ namaḥ; at the tips of the toes of the right foot—Ṇaṃ namaḥ;
at the root of the left thigh—Taṃ namaḥ; at the left knee—Thaṃ namaḥ.
On the left ankle—*daṃ namaḥ*; at the base of the toes of the left foot—*dhaṃ namaḥ*; on the tips of the toes of the left foot—*naṃ namaḥ*;
on the ten sides—*paṃ namaḥ*;
on the left side—*phaṃ namaḥ*; on the back—*baṃ namaḥ*; at the navel—*bhaṃ namaḥ*.
In the stomach—*maṃ* *namaḥ*.
One should place [the syllables] one above the other from the heart up to the throat:
*yaṃ* *namaḥ*, *raṃ* *namaḥ*, *laṃ* *namaḥ*, *vaṃ* *namaḥ*.

*Śaṃ* namaḥ, *ṣaṃ* namaḥ, *saṃ* namaḥ, *haṃ* namaḥ, *laṃ* namaḥ, *kṣaṃ* namaḥ—thus one should place these ten seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the elements at the beginning of the [consonant] groups. This is the external placement of the Mātṛkās (*bahirmātṛkānyāsa*). Having meditated thus, O Sovereign of the Gods, one should thereafter perform the twofold placement (*nyāsa*), beginning with Bālā and beginning with the Root-mantra (*mūla*).
Having performed the creation beginning with Kāmā and Ramā, one should perform the placement (nyāsa):

*oṃ 3 aiṃ klīṃ sauṃ aṃ namaḥ* from the hairline (*keśānta*) and so forth; the root mantra *aṃ namaḥ* from the hairline and so forth; *hrīṃ a namaḥ*, *klīṃ aṃ namaḥ*, *śrīṃ aṃ namaḥ*, and *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* from the middle of the forehead to the sole of the foot.

Hand purification is performed by repeating twice over the fingers. Or, it is done by mutual touching of the left and right palms and the backs of the hands. This hand-purifying *vidyā*, extending from the middle finger to the base of the palm, repeated twice over the fingers, is the purification of the hands, O Dear One.

First, the Keśavādi-mātṛkā-nyāsa: Here, having recollected the seer and other components—namely, Sādhyanārāyaṇa as the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī as the meter (*chandas*), and Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa as the deity (*devatā*)—and having performed the assignment (*vinyasya*) with the thought, "The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of this nyāsa as a limb of my Śrīvidyā," one should perform the hand and limb assignments (*karāṅga-nyāsa*). *Khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya ddholkāya svāhā śrīdevyai hṛdayāya namaḥ; oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ so'haṃ iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya maholkāya svāhā śrīṃ padminyai namaḥ śirase svāhā.*

Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ sohaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya vīrolkāya svāhā śrūṃ viṣṇupatnyai śikhāyai vaṣaṭ. Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ sohaṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ oṃ namo.

To Nārāyaṇa, who is like lightning and a meteor, Svāhā! Śrīṃ, to the Giver of Boons, for the armor, Huṃ!—Oṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, Haṃsaḥ So’haṃ Oṃ (Oṃ) Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ Auṃ Hrīṃ, Haṃsaḥ So’haṃ Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, to the one with a thousand meteors, Svāhā! Śrīṃ, to her whose form is the lotus of desire, for the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ!—Oṃ Śrīṃ Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa.

Having applied the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*)— namely *haṃsaḥ so'haṃ*, *aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ*, *hrīḥ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ*, *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya anantolkāya svāhā*, *śraḥ śūlinyai*, and *astrāya phaṭ*— to both hands from the thumbs to the palms, and having likewise applied them to the six limbs beginning with the heart, one should meditate as follows:

The unbroken embodiment of the Self, whose hands are beautified by the *vidyā* lotus, the mirror, the jar of nectar, the *padma*, the *kaumodakī* mace, and the *sudarśana* discus, shines forth as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, possessing the radiant luster of lightning and the moon.
The word "body" (*vapuḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. One should meditate on the weapons starting from the lower left hand up to the lower right hand.
Having thus meditated—[on] the mirror (*mukura*), the *ādarśa*, the conch (*dara*), and the *śaṅkha*—one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*):
*oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ keśavāya kīrtyai namaḥ* on the forehead.

*klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ viṣṇave dhṛtyai namaḥ* on the right ear. In this manner, the mantra is to be enclosed by the three seed-syllables preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the *tritārā* (three stars) in all instances. 4. *ūṃ madhusūdanāya śāntyai namaḥ* on the left ear.
