Śrī Aiṃ Iṃ Īṃ Ūṃ Saṅketasāra-mūlavidyāmbā.
6 hrīṃ bhagavatī vicce vāgvādini klīṃ mahāhṛdayamāyāmātaṅgini aiṃ klinne blūṃ strīṃ anutaravāgvādinī mūlavidyāmbā śrī0, 6 shauṃḥ hsauṃḥ hskhphreṃ hsklīṃ hsauṃḥ anutaraśāṅkarī.

6 hsauṃḥ shauṃḥ ha sa ka la ha sa ka ha la sa ka la hrīṃ: O Parāmṛta-Śakti, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, residing in the Bindu-cakra consisting of the bliss of emission; Sovereign of all mantras, Sovereign of all yantras, Sovereign of all cakras, Sovereign of all pīṭhas, Sovereign of all vidyās, Sovereign of all speech!
May all the sovereigns of yoga, the sovereigns of all accomplishments, the Mothers who are the source of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire world—
along with their wheels (*cakra*), deities, mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, retinues, and wheel-ladies— be worshipped and gratified with all ritual offerings; homage!
"Śrī Mahātripurasundarī Mūlavidyāmbā Śrī," thus [worshipping] the sixteen Root-Vidyās;
having worshipped and gratified the Goddesses with the Root-Mantra (mūla), at the Mūlādhāra: "6 Haṃsaḥ svātmānandavibhūtyai svāhā, Mūlādhāravidyāmbā Śrī"; at the Svādhiṣṭhāna: "6 So'haṃ..."
To the glory of the Paramahaṃsa, Svāhā! Śrī Svādhiṣṭhāna-Vidyāmbā. At Maṇipūra: 6 Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ, to the Supreme Self, the Pure Bliss Paramahaṃsa, Svāhā!
Śrī Maṇipūraka-Vidyāmbā. At Anāhata: 6 Haṃ Saḥ, awaken my own Self!
To Awakening: Śrī Anāhatātmavidyāmbā; in the Viśuddhi [cakra]:
for the sake of the contemplation of the true nature of *haṃsa*, Śrī Viśuddhavidyāmbā; in the Ājñā [cakra]:
*haṃ saḥ so'haṃ svāhā*, for the sake of the nectar of the light of consciousness which is pure bliss, Svāhā Ājñāvidyāmbā.

Śrī0 6—Having thus thrice gratified the Goddess with the root-mantra of the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra), [one recites]: Śrī0 6 *yo'ham asmi brahmāham asmi* (I who am, I am Brahman) for the aspect of Light (*prakāśacaraṇa*); Śrī0 6 *aham asmi brahmāham asmi* (I am, I am Brahman) for the aspect of Reflection (*vimarśacaraṇa*);
Śrī0 6 *so'ham* (That I am) for the aspect of Light-and-Reflection (*prakāśavimarśacaraṇa*); Śrī0 6 *yo'ham asmi brahmāham asmi aham asmi*.

"I am Brahmā, O Śrī, whose feet are the Nirvāṇa that is completely full of pure light. Having satiated the Goddess three times with the root mantra and having propitiated her through all ritual actions, one should contemplate the state of Unmanī, the supportless, void state, thinking "I am He" (*so'ham asmi*). Thus, [one contemplates] one's own Self.

Meditating on the form of Śiva, which transcends the universe and consists of self-luminous consciousness, one should satisfy the Goddess with the root mantra according to one's capacity. Then, having worshipped as before with offerings beginning with *pādya* and ending with incense, lamps, and food (*naivedya*), one should draw a mandala in the northeastern quarter of the *cakra* as previously described, [reciting]: "Oṃ, salutation to the all-pervading mandala."

Having thus performed the worship, one should establish the five aforementioned maṇḍalas in that [space]— in the east, south, west, north, and center— and having visualized them, one should place five vessels together with their bases, containing water mixed with food and side-dishes; [one should then visualize] the maṇḍalas of Fire, Sun, and Moon within the bases, the vessels, and the substances.

Having worshipped in the west with "Bāṃ, obeisance to Baṭukanātha," and having displayed the *kapāla-yoni-mudrā*, [one recites]: "O Devīputra Baṭukanātha, radiant with a mass of tawny matted locks, tawny-eyed and three-eyed, accept, accept this worship and offering, svāhā! [One offers] with the nectar from the vessel of offerings.

Having gratified [the deity] in the form of a continuous stream with the left thumb and ring finger, and having taken a handful of flowers, may Baṭuka— who is satisfied by the offering of the bali, who bestows all perfections,
and who is attended by bhūtas and vetālas— grant me constant peace.

Having thus cast forth a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. This is the *baṭukabali*. To the north: having worshelled with "OṂ YĀṂ NAMO YOGINĪBHYAḤ," [one offers to] OṂ YĀṂ to the Yoginīs, to all beings (*sarvabhūta*), to those who pay homage to the Lord of All Beings (*sarvabhūtādhipati*), and to the Śākinīs.
To those who dwell in the three worlds, accept, accept this offering and oblation, svāhā!

Having gratified [the deities] with the stream of nectar from the vessel of the offering using the left thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers, and taking a handful of flowers, [recite]: oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ.
Whatever yoginīs there may be—whether fierce, gentle, most terrible, or supreme;
whether moving through the sky, moving on the earth, or moving in the void—may they always be pleased with me.

Having thus cast a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*; this is the offering to the Yoginīs (*yoginī-bali*). In the east: having worshipped with "Sāṃ, obeisance to all beings" (*sāṃ sarvabhūtebhyo namaḥ*), [one recites]:
"Sāṃ, obeisance to all beings; svāhā to the lords of all beings! Accept, accept this worship and offering, svāhā!"
Having gratified [the deities] with a stream of nectar from the vessel of offerings using all the fingers of the left hand, and taking up a handful of flowers, [one recites]:
"Those beings of various forms who dwell in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space,
as well as those residing in the depths of the netherworld, who are purified by the yoga of Śiva."

May Dhruva and the others, as well as Indra and the others stationed in their respective directions—those who are true to their vows—be satisfied with joyful minds; may these beings accept this bali offering.
Having thus cast a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and prostrated with the *yonimudrā*, this is the offering to the spirits (*bhūtabali*).
To the south: having worshipped with "4 *kṣāṃ* obeisance to Kṣetrapāla," [one recites] "4 *kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*. Come, come, O Goddess-son Baṭukanātha, you who take away the remnants!"
"Again and again, destroy, destroy the Jaina mendicants, the guardians of the field, and all obstacles!
Accept, accept this offering along with all ritual services, svāhā!
Having thus satisfied them with a stream of nectar from the vessel of the *bali* offering using the left thumb and forefinger, [one should proceed].
Taking this handful of flowers, may the servant of the Guardian of the Field who dwells in this sacred precinct,
being pleased by this offering, grant me protection from all dangers.
Thus, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. This is the *bali* offering to the Guardian of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*).
In the center: having worshipped with "Oṃ [four times] obeisance to Rājarājeśvara," [one worships] with "Oṃ [four times] Aiṃ Hsauṃḥ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ, to the one presided over by Yugāntabhairava."

For the sake of attaining the desired siddhi of Akṣobhya, Ānanda, and Hṛdaya, descend, descend! O Great Teacher Kṣetrapāla, son of the Goddess Baṭukanātha, son of noble lineage, son of the Mother, son of the Siddhas;
O Lord of this place, Lord of this region, Lord of this village—[accept] this worship and this bali offering.
Seize, seize! Make firm, make firm! Grind, grind! Crush, crush! Blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up!
Destroy, destroy all obstacles! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ! To the Kṣetrapāla, vauṣaṭ!
O Sovereign Lord of the Kings of the Kṣetrapālas, [named] Amuka, accept, accept this worship and this offering, svāhā!
Having gratified [the deities] with a stream of nectar from the offering vessel using the left thumb and middle finger, and taking a handful of flowers, [one recites]: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ;
by this offering of the bali, may [the deity], accompanied by the host of *baṭus*, [be satisfied]*.
May the Lord, the King of Kings of kings, be gracious to me at all times.

Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*; this is the *bali* offering to Rājarājeśvarī. Having satiated the Goddess three times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and having performed the dismissal of the water and food offerings as before, one should offer betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) with the root mantra.
Now follows the procedure for the special *ārārtika* offering:
A wise person should draw a wheel in the center of a vessel made of gold or other materials;
having filled it with rice, he should then arrange it into nine sections.
Immediately thereafter, having fashioned nine balls in the shape of wheels,
he prepared pairs of *maṇḍaka* cakes filled with sugar.
The specific *ghaṭikās* should be prepared... [omitted] ...one should apply nine *ghaṭikās* in a manner of seven times seven.
Having placed the balls upon the eight corners, one should cast them over;
then, having displayed the wheel-gesture (cakramudrā), one should scatter lamps cooked in ghee.
One should place fist-mudrās in the shape of svastikas here and there.
Then, having lit lamps for Bhuvaneśvarī with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ*, one should worship her with the nine jewels. [The mantra is:
*hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ glūṃ sluṃ mlūṃ plūṃ nlūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*—this is the Pañcaratnavidyā.
One should worship in the four directions and in the center. In the east, one should worship: *hsrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ ūrmiṇyai namaḥ*.
In the south: *aiṃ klinne klīṃ madadrave kule hsrauṃ bhoginyai namaḥ*.

In the west, one should worship Kubjikā with: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsphreṃ hsauṃ bhagavatyamba hsphreṃ hskhphreṃ kubjike [hsrūṃ srhūṃ] aghore ghore aghoramukhi chrāṃ chrīṃ kiṇi kiṇi [hrsauṃ hsphreṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ] kubjikāyai*.
Homage!
One should worship Kālikā in the north—thus one should worship with: *khphreṃ mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī kālikāyai namaḥ*.
There, one should worship the five lion-throne vidyās. In front of that, one should recite the hymn to the host of goddesses,
lifting it up from the head nine times again.
Thereafter, one should establish the great splendor consisting of a garland of lamps.
At the end of the root mantra:
"O Goddess Navātmikā, joined with the entire assembly of the wheels and their sovereigns;
O Goddess, accept this waving of lights for my success."
This is the mantra.

O Dear One, one should meditate with a perfectly steady gaze upon the ritual of the *ārātrika* offering. Thus concludes the specific procedure for the *ārātrika* that grants all desires. Then, taking a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), [one should proceed].
O Sundarī, O supreme deity, O you who shine with various ornaments, O you of stainless auspiciousness, be gracious toward me;
you who dwell near the divine sandals made of the finest celestial jewels!
This handful of flowers has been offered as praise composed by Viriñci, the Earth.

Having thus offered a handful of flowers at the feet of the Goddess, [he beheld her] accompanied by the celestial chariot, the parasol, the fly-whisks, and the hosts of sages such as Nārada, along with gods, dānavas, gandharvas,
kiṃnaras, kimpuruṣas, yakṣas, siddhas, sādhyas, vidyādharas, and apsarases.

Having offered the royal services (*rājopacāra*) to the Goddess with the words, "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, please attend to the practitioners through the great festivals of dance, song, instrumental music, and actors," one should perform the worship of the Yoginīs.
Having drawn a hexagonal mandala on one's left side, [one should worship] with perfumes, unbroken grains, and flowers.

Having adorned [the deity] and performed the worship of the yoga-seat in brief, one should invoke the Goddess upon that seat as before, worship her with all the ritual services beginning with invocation, satisfy the Yoginī five times with the root mantra, and meditate:
In her hair she consists of peacock feathers; in her face, of moonlight; in her teeth, of pearls;
in her conversation, of nectar; on her pair of arms, of Mandāra garlands;
on her neck, of conchs; on her breast, of mountains; and she who is [composed] of swans— [May that Lakṣmī grant you prosperity.]
O daughter of the Lord of the Mind, dwell in my heart, which is like the middle of the sky.
This wine-vessel, accompanied by flesh, is offered to you;
having accepted it, O auspicious Goddess, grant me victory and consume my enemies.
Thus one should give the vessel of power (*śaktipātra*) to the Yoginī.
Having bowed to the independent Girijā and having displayed the mudrās with flowers—
[and] having taken up the cause, one should offer oblations to the Guru and Bhavānī with the mantra.
Furthermore, one should offer the fourfold reality with the substances contained in the vessel:
"O Supreme Mistress, easily accessible through devotion, who delights in the essence of supreme nectar!
Grant me the remainder of this vessel filled with Your gracious glance; have mercy!"
Having thus prayed, [he said]:
"O child, this nectar of the lineage, the remains of what I have drunk, is given by me to you.
I shall destroy your enemies and grant you every desire."

Thus, having received from the hand of the Yoginī the vessel of her sidelong glance and accepted it, and having given her the remaining food of the offering and betel, [he reflected: "For those whose feet stumble upon the ground, the earth alone is the support."
Born dependent upon others, you alone are my refuge.

Having thus prayed and displayed the five mudrās, and considering the Goddess to have arrived at the seat upon one’s head, one should place the flower from her feet upon one’s own head and dismiss her. Then, having satisfied one’s own guru three times with the *pādukā* mantra, one should offer [the remains] to him. With one’s own vessel, [one should satisfy] oneself.
Having satisfied [the deities] three times, one should unite [them] within oneself. Thus ends the worship of the Yoginīs.
Thus concludes the seventh chapter in the *Svacchandapaddhati* composed by the venerable Cidānandanātha.

Then, having worshipped the deities of the ritual occasion according to the scriptures and according to the instructions of the guru, one should honor and satisfy them as follows: "Obeisance to Jñāna and the others, the founders of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman, the ancestral sages; obeisance to the gurus."
The triad of gurus beginning with Śrīnātha [resides] in the thousand-petaled lotus,
the supreme bliss of Brahman.
O Guru of the World, when does the yogi become a seeker of the root-kanda, and when does he become an enjoyer in the city of Vārāṇasī?
O compassionate one, I bow to the illustrious Vimalānanda, the one whose bliss is stainless.
Amṛtānanda,
having deliberated, [entrusted it] to Śiva, who is skilled in his own doctrine and whose nature is auspiciousness.
You alone are the Guru, the state of consciousness-bliss; from the aspect of consciousness, I am [the disciple].
By whose grace I [attain] the ocean of consciousness and the bliss of consciousness.
Enough with conceptual constructions;
I pay homage to the feet of the Guru,
which are like space, wind, and fire.
Hari alone is the family dharma,
free from all that is visible.

[Homage to] all the deities residing in the Śrīcakra of the Yoginīs— the most secret of secrets, the *nigarbha*, *kulakaula*, *rahasya*, *paramarahasya*, and *atirahasya* belonging to the entire tradition of the manifest, the hidden, and the most hidden;
[homage to] the venerable Guru, the venerable Paramaguru.
4 Parameṣṭhiguru Śrī, 4 Parātparaguru Śrī,
4 Śuddhavidyāmbā Śrī, 4 Bālātripurasundarī Śrī, 4 Śrīmahātripurasundarī Śrī, 4 Rājamātaṅgī Śrī.
4 Tiraṣkariṇyambā Śrī, 4 Lopāmudrāmbā Śrī,
4 Saubhāgyavidyāmbā Śrī, 4 Turyāmbā Śrī, 4 Turyāmbāśrī, 4 Rājarājeśvaryambā Śrī.
4 Parāśriyamvā Śrī, 4 Parāprāsādāmvā Śrī,
4 Prāsādaparāmvā Śrī, 4 Parābhaṭṭārikāmvā Śrī, 4 Śūlinīdurgāmvā Śrī, 4 Parāśāmbhavyamvā Śrī.
4 Laghuśāmalāmbā Śrī, 4 Anuttaraparāmbā Śrī, 4 Vāsudevānanda Śrī, 4 Paramahaṃsānanda Śrī,
4 Dattātreya Śrī, 4 Gopālakṛṣṇa Śrī.
To Cidānandeśvara Śrī, 4; to Mahābaleśvara Śrī, 4;
to Mahākālī Śrī, 4; to all the deities residing within the Śrīcakra Śrī, 4;
to all the gods Śrī, 4; to all the Brāhmaṇas Śrī, 4.
Having worshipped the triad of lineages (*oghatriya*) with the mantras "Obeisance to the Supreme Mother, the embodiment of all deities, Śrī... and "Obeisance to Brahmā and the others, Śrī...",
and having performed the salutation to the Guru with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), [one proceeds] by the Guru's permission.

Reciting the mantras taught by their own gurus, they should sit down. Then the Ācārya, having satiated the Goddess three times with the root mantra, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before, and having performed the assignment of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth,
as well as the six-limbed assignment (kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), and having meditated upon himself in the form of the Goddess, [should recite] according to his capacity.
Having recited [the mantra], one should offer it. Having recited the hymn to the Guru and the hymn to the Goddess:
"I take refuge in that certain deity who is the Lord arisen from the sequence of all powers, whose great nature is delusion, and who consists of the bliss of consciousness."
Thus, by means of the *yonimudrā*,
whatever sins there may be are [purified] at every step through circumambulation.
With the two knees, as well as the feet, chest, head, eyes,
two hands, mind, and speech— the prostration with eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) is thus described.
With both knees, hands, chest, head, and voice—
this five-limbed prostration is the most excellent form of worship according to the ritual rules.
Having thus prostrated,
one should display these five mudrās at the conclusion of the worship: the Stambhana, the Caturasra, the Matsya, the Gokhura, and the Yoni-mudrā.
The practitioner indeed commits an offense at every step;
who else in this world, save for the Mistress alone, can endure it?

Having thus asked for forgiveness in many ways preceded by prostrations, and having taken the general *arghya* water in another vessel, [one recites]: "Whatever [wrong] was done by me previously, through the authority of my life-force, intellect, body, and duties, in the states of waking,
dreaming, and deep sleep, by means of mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the stomach,"
Whatever has been thought, spoken, or done by me— let all that be an offering to the venerable Guru and the Deity,
svāhā! O Śivā, whatever is performed by me, whether knowingly or unknowingly...
Considering all this to be your own work, please forgive me.
Whether good or bad, whatever action has been performed by me,
O Goddess, please accept all of it as my worship out of compassion.

Having thus whirled the conch above the Goddess, one should pour [the water] slightly toward the northeast. Taking the remaining water in the hand, having stirred it for the sake of worship, and having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should sprinkle oneself with it and sprinkle the Sāmans once.
May those great goddesses, who are in the form of rays and are the deities worshipped in the wheel,
being united with the limbs of Śrī Sundarī, always bring about auspiciousness.

Having thus placed a flower upon the head and meditated upon oneself in the form of the Goddess, [one performs] the Khecarī [mudrā]. Having prostrated to the Goddess with her seed-syllable (bīja), and at the end of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) saying "O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, forgive me," one should address the Goddess with three claps of the hands (tāla) and contemplate Her as consisting of pure light.
Go, go to the supreme abode, your own place, O Supreme Goddess,
where even the gods beginning with Brahmā do not know that highest state.

One should cause it to reach the thousand-petaled lotus located at the head by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*. Then, having brought it to the heart-lotus via the path of the *suṣumṇā* with the mantra "Aiṃ, obeisance to the heart" (p. 253), [one should perform the placement].
Stay, stay, O Supreme Goddess, in that supreme abode which is your own natural place,
where all the gods beginning with Brahmā abide within my heart.
Having worshipped the Supreme Deity, who resides in the center of the Śrīcakra as described, with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) in one's heart,

one should establish her in the Mūlādhāra. Then, upon a triangular maṇḍala in the northeast, [one should visualize her] as one who delights in the entertainment of lute-playing and song, and who is clothed in a blue garment.

I bow to the goddess Mātaṅgī, who has lips like the *bimba* fruit, feet moist with fresh lac, and tresses adorned with flowers; she is slender-limbed, wearing earrings of white conch shells, radiant with ornaments of rubies, possessing a smiling face, and as pure as a parrot.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with the *nirmālya* flowers: "4 Aiṃ! Obeisance to Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī Mātaṅgī, the subduer of all, Svāhā! 4 [Obeisance to] Śeṣikāśrīpādukā. Having thus worshipped with the *nirmālya* water, having offered libations, and having presented the remainder of the food offering (*naivedya*).
Taking the offered flowers (nirmālya),
as well as foods to be licked and sucked, drinks, betel, garlands, and ointments— I give this offering of the remains (nirmālya-bhojana) to you by the command of Śrī Śiva.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should prostrate with the *yonimudrā*. This is the procedure for the worship of Śeṣikā.

In that very place, saying "Salutation to the attendants of the Goddess," one should scatter the remaining water from the worship, along with flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth, upon the ground. Then, preceded by three claps of the hands (*tāla*), [one recites]: *ūṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
O Lord of gods, O Guru, O Master, O Teacher, O Self, O Leader!
Save me, save me! Make this worship most complete.
Having thus prayed, one should lift the *śrīpātra* up to the level of the head, satisfy the Guru situated upon the crown of the head,
and place that vessel upon the base (*ādhāra*). Having poured a little of that water into the *śāntipātra*,
one should take the *ātmapātra* with both hands and perform the fourfold reality (*tattvacatuṣṭaya*).
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Svacchandapaddhati* composed by the illustrious Cidānandanātha. (p.
255) Thereafter, one should bestow the fourfold reality (*tattvacatuṣṭaya*) upon those who have been initiated according to the scripture and who observe the rules of conduct (*sāmayika*).
It is as follows:
4 Aiṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ klīṃ ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ sauṃḥ sakalahrīṃ.
O Thou who art inflamed by the oblation of dharma and adharma, with the mind as the ladle, I perpetually offer the functioning of the senses into the two selves by way of the *suṣumnā* path. Svāhā!
Thus, the Ācārya, having offered his own vessel into the vessel of the Guru and into himself, the initiates (sāmayika) should request the *prasāda* from the Ācārya:
"O Śrīnātha, O Śrīmatānnātha, O Compassionate One, O You who are kind to devotees!"
By the sight of your feet, protect me from the ocean of worldly existence.
The pair of feet of the glorious Guru is forever situated upon my head;
salutations to the Guru, who is the embodiment of all and is known as both Light (prakāśa) and Reflective Awareness (vimarśa).
O Lord, Protector, Guru, Master! May the auspicious grace of the Guru and the Goddess, which brings about well-being, be bestowed upon us. Grant us that which is conducive to our welfare.
Then, one should give the *prasāda*— the remainder remaining in one’s own vessel— to all [the deities],
beginning with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, speech, hands,
feet, anus, and genitals; and sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, and so forth.

By means of the impure principle (aśuddhatattva) of the self, [with the seed-syllables] aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ aiṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ, I purify the gross body, which is the principle of the self (ātmatattva). This body, known as "gross," is the witness to the equilibrium of the fourteen sense organs and their objects.
The reality of the ten parts of the bestower of Dharma is to be purified by the fire whose essence is the syllable *Aiṃ*: *Aiṃ Ka E Ī La Hrīṃ*.
O You who possess the form of Kula, place here the spontaneous manifestation within the supreme nectar-self that produces the bliss of the undivided single flavor!
*Hail to Mukunda, whose essence is the syllable *Aiṃ*, who consists of ten digits (*kalā*) that bestow the Dharma, who takes the form of the circle of fire (*vahnimaṇḍala*),
who is skilled in severing the knots of all living beings, who is the universal Vaiśvānara, whose form is the Virāṭ-sthūla-body,
who dwells in the first section, and who is the root-tuber of Kuṇḍalinī.* *Svāhā!*
This salutation is to Mukunda.
The serpent-king’s coil is his support; the circle of the earth is his vessel;
the waters of the seven oceans are the offering; and the elephants of the eight directions are his attendants.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining one's desired goals, I shall worship Bhairava every day with flowers protected by the hosts of stars and the nine planets beginning with the Sun.

4. Māyā, Vidyā, Kalā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, and Puruṣa— by way of these, as pure and impure, [are represented by] kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ klīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ.

I purify the subtle body by means of the *vidyā-tattva*; purify! The body known as the subtle, which consists of the form of the individual soul (*jīvatva*) and the equilibrium of the fourteen sense organs, is to be purified by the solar radiance consisting of the syllable *klīṃ* and the *tattva* of the twelve digits that bestow objects; *klīṃ*.
Ha Sa Ka Ha La Hrīṃ!
O You who abide in Akula, whose form is nectar, who bestows the knowledge of accomplishment,
O Supreme One, O You whose nature is moist, bestow the state of immortality upon this object!

Salutations to the one whose essence is the syllable *klīṃ*, who consists of twelve digits that bestow wealth, who is the form of the solar orb, who is skilled in piercing the knot of *rajas*, who is the nature of the thread of fire (*taijasa-sūtra*),
who is the subtle body of Hiraṇyagarbha, who dwells in the second section, and who is the form of Kuṇḍalinī.
To Brahman, Svāhā! This is for Brahman; let it be offered. 4.
Svā— [Oblation] to the one situated in the corner, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, whose form is consciousness in the shape of Kuṇḍalī; I offer this... kam.
I, whose nature is Śiva, offer into the fire of my own supreme "I-consciousness" this supreme nectar consisting of the "this-ness" that is filled with the vessel of egoity.

By means of the Vidyā-tattva, consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā, with the syllables yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ sauḥ, and the mantra *sakalahrīṃ*, I purify, do thou purify, the causal body by means of the Śiva-tattva. [The state of] equilibrium of the three qualities of the elements...
The body, known as the causal [body], consisting of the sixteen kalās that bestow desire and having the nature of the syllable *sauḥ*,
is to be purified. Having made the *sauḥ*— which consists of all the *hrīṃ*s— your own form, you become identical with that very essence through the offering of water (*arghya*).
Having assumed the form of the nectar of the Kula, cause the vibration of consciousness to arise within me.

To the one whose essence is the syllable *sauḥ*, the bestower of desires, the self of the sixteen digits; to the one skilled in shattering the knots of *tamas*; to the one whose form is the lunar orb; to the one who is the unmanifest causal body of the syllable of wisdom (*prajñākṣara*);
to the one dwelling in the third section; to the one whose form is the great light shining at the tip of the crest of Kuṇḍalinī.

Svāhā to Bhadramūrti Paśupati! This [offering] is for Paśupati, not mine. [I offer praise to] Śivā, who awakens one to the coming and passing away of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; who is both terrible and peaceful; and who transcends the five states beginning with delusion.
One should know that which is defined as the limit of negation expressed by the words "not this, not this," and which is made known through various doctrines, by means of service to the Teacher.
[She is] that digit consisting of pure experience, which transcends the bindu, nāda, and kalā, whose nature is indivisible bliss,
and which is entirely free from the flood of conceptual constructions.
By constantly meditating on that which dwells within the midst of the interval of bliss,
I shall become of its very form, by the command of the supreme king of true teachers.

4. [The sequence] by way of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), hearing (*śrotra*), touch (*tvak*), sight (*cakṣus*), taste (*jihvā*), smell (*ghrāṇa*), speech (*vāk*), hands (*pāṇi*), feet (*pāda*), excretory organ (*pāyu*), generative organ (*upastha*), sound (*śabda*), touch (*sparśa*), form (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), smell (*gandha*), ether (*ākāśa*), wind (*vāyu*), fire (*vahni*), water (*salila*), earth (*bhūmi*), *māyā*, *kalā*, *vidyā*, passion (*rāga*), time (*kāla*), necessity (*niyati*), the person (*puruṣa*), Śiva, power (*śakti*), Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

By means of all the principles (*tattva*): aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ.

Śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ aiṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ klīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sauḥ sakalahrīṃ. I purify with all the principles (tattvas) the individual soul (jīva), which consists of the thirty-six principles and is the substratum of the three bodies—the gross, the subtle, and the causal; purify it! O Being-Consciousness-Bliss, Equanimity, the One Non-dual!

The body named the Fourth State of Divine Bliss (*divyānanda-turya*), which consists of the three causal [bodies], is to be purified by the consciousness of omniscience and other qualities. *Aiṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ klīṃ hasakahalahrīṃ sauḥ sakalahrīṃ*.
That which is the existence of the universe manifested by Consciousness—by that universal existence, one should realize: "I am Śiva."
"I am the Lord," thus constantly breathing, I am fearless; I am unrestrained.
When the fire of consciousness— which blazes within without interval, which consumes the fuel of delusion, and which is the adversary of the darkness of ignorance—
has become the ground for the expansion of its wondrous rays...
I offer the universe—the earth, the directions, and the very limits of the world—into the fire.
Crushed by the Mandara mountain of wisdom, the great ocean of existence was churned;

through the revolutions caused by the casting of the churning-stick, the nectar of immortality was respectfully extracted from all sides. Having cast aside the multitude of the pride of the Daityas, it disregarded the transience of worldly prosperity.
Those who drink even the dregs again and again are the ones praised in the world as true immortals.

Svāhā to Sadāśiva, who is the self of all reality, the self of all kalās, the self of all maṇḍalas; who is skilled in severing all knots, who dwells in all parts, whose form is the entire body, who is the form of the beginning, middle, end, and conclusion, and who consists of the five praṇavas.
Salutation to Sadāśiva.
I am the Haṃsa, the Śiva, eternally heard as the partless (niṣkala);
I am the blazing consciousness, the experience of blissful awareness.
I am the Lord; I am the one of firm resolve established by the Vedas;
I am that very Self; all this is "I am Śiva. || 1 ||
Having meditated upon that form with a great mind imbued with the nectar of the glorious mass of awakening, I constantly [visualize] it as having the luster of a thousand-petaled moon-disc;
then, having brought that very Guru to the sixteen-petaled [lotus], I contemplate him as being of the nature of mantra.
Meditating within the interior of the heart-lotus, one should thus remember the venerable Guru as being identical with that very Self.
Having traversed the forest consisting of sound and other sense objects, he engaged in a terrifying battle with that very self which consists of horses and so forth.
The host of demons such as passion and the like is swiftly destroyed. || 3 ||
Having constructed a mental bridge for the body and swiftly crossed the ocean of saṃsāra,
he indeed destroyed passion, hatred, and the other [afflictions].
Endowed with tranquility, he shines in his own bliss. || 4 ||
Having swiftly crossed the ocean of saṃsāra at that very moment by means of you,
I have slain Rāvaṇa, who was born of ignorance.
One should joyfully cultivate the bliss born of meditative concentration. || 5 ||
O mind, ascend this river of the six flavors;
having relied upon the weighty words of Janaka, cross over it completely.
Thus, within the multitude of worldly existences, I have conquered the six great enemies.
In the ancient dwelling of the Enemy of Tripura, the drum of victory is being beaten.
"I am that very Consciousness"—thus known through the statement "I am Brahman.
I am pure Being alone, beyond the range of objects, non-dual, the eternal witness of the mind;
I am Truth, Knowledge, beginningless Awareness, stainless, the form of supreme wisdom, and the Great One.
Thus, the state of samādhi is a mass of the bliss of Brahman, higher than the highest.
Even while living, I am Śiva by virtue of the word of the true Guru; through the powers of knowledge and action, and by means of the manifested knowledge, I move about like an ordinary person.
Upon the exhaustion of the enjoyment of all good and evil fruits born from the entire web of commenced karma—
When this body has fallen, that very Self is the Lord of the world of moving and non-moving beings.
Like a crystal staff within and a staff of wood without,
the virtuous constantly perceive me as the light both inside and out.
By your grace, O Śrī Guru, I am that supreme reality—consisting of consciousness and bliss—which is manifest as both internal and external, and beyond; of this there is no doubt.
O Supreme Bliss whose nature is knowledge and whose essence is the eternally manifest form!
By the power of your grace, may I become manifest Consciousness-Bliss. 11.
Salutations to the Guru, the piercer of the Vedānta, the witness of all, whose nature is the light of the inner self, and whose form is the foundation of the universe. 12.
Through the abandonment of the delusion of the body, [one attains] infinite, imperishable bliss;
because it is my own true nature, I am the imperishable consciousness-bliss. || 13 ||
Consisting of the essence of the experience of tasting the nectar of Brahman-bliss, it was created by Cidānanda for the benefit of the worlds. (14)
Who that is mortal would not be satiated while drinking this non-dual nectar flowing from the lotus-face of Consciousness-Bliss, which provides easy crossing over the ocean of worldly existence? 15.
I have assumed this body for the sake of awakening to the bliss of consciousness, becoming a bee at the lotus feet of Nanda, the lord of yogis.
Whatever I do from morning until evening, and from evening until morning, O Source of the Universe, may that be an act of worship unto You. (17)

From this point forward, may whatever has been thought, done, or intended by me—with mind, speech, or action; with the hands, feet, belly, or genitals—during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, throughout my life, body, and duties, all of that be offered to the venerable Guru and the Deity; Svāhā! Oṃ Aiṃ.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ!
For the satisfaction of all the gods and for the stabilization of the knowledge of Brahman—[he who], while serving [them], consumes honey and meat out of craving, is a sinner. Svāhā!
Just as a house enveloped in darkness is seen by means of a lamp, so indeed the Self, shrouded by illusion, is seen by means of the divine drink. Svāhā!
4. The form of the blissful Brahman is that which is established within the body.
Wine is its manifestor; therefore it is drunk by yogins. Svāhā! 4.
Oṃ, I am the moist, blazing light; I am the light that blazes, I am Brahman.
I who am this, I am Brahman; I am this, I am Brahman; I alone am I, I offer myself—Svāhā!
May the universe— from Śiva down to the earth, including all from Brahmā to a blade of grass,
and from Kālāgni up to Śiva— be satisfied by this sacrifice.
Oṃ. Fullness is from fullness; this is fullness. From fullness, fullness issues forth. When fullness is taken from fullness, fullness alone remains.
Having invoked with "Oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ," one should perform the dismissal of the bali offering (*balivisarjana*).
Therein, having taken the substances from the bali vessel that was set out into a single vessel, holding a water-filled vessel in one's hand—

Having gone outside the house, one should prepare a maṇḍala in a clean place as before and meditate upon Bhairava, who has the luster of blackness, possesses three eyes, and holds a mace, a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a vessel in his hands— this is the protection (*nivāraṇa*). *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ.* One should meditate on Bhairava, who is dark-hued, has three eyes, and holds a mace, a trident, a *ḍamaru*, and a vessel in his hands— this is the warding off [of obstacles].

Having meditated thus, one should offer the oblation (bali) contained in the vessel with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ 4 ucchiṣṭabhairava ehyehi baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*. Then, having discarded that vessel and washed both hands and feet, one should go to the door of the worship chamber and, saying "May there be prosperity," enter within the house.
Having added a little water to the substances contained in the *śāntipātra*, one should sprinkle oneself, the *Śakti*, and the initiates (*sāmayika*) with it while reciting the *Śāntistava*:
"May the Goddesses who dwell at the lotus-feet of Hara be victorious!"
I bow to the eight groups of eight Yoginīs, who are gracious, bestowers of the nectar of liberation, and awakeners of the intellect regarding the infinite Siddhānta. 1.
I bow my head to the Lord Bhairava, the beloved of Bhairavī, who stands in the midst of the circle of Yoginīs and is surrounded by the Mothers. 2.
May all calamities, misfortunes, and diseases resulting from the transgression of conventional conduct be dispelled through union with the divine Śrīcakra. (3)
May there be long life, health, sovereignty, fame, prosperity, happiness, and victory; may there be beauty and the fulfillment of all desires, and may all the deities protect [you]. (4)

May the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Family, grant peace to those who worship Him, those who observe His injunctions, those who have conquered their senses, and those whose wealth is austerity; and may He grant peace to the land, the kingdom, the lineage, and the king. 5.
May all practitioners rejoice; may detractors perish.
May the state of Śambhu be mine, and may my Guru always be gracious. (6)
May the lineage of teachers belonging to the family of practitioners rejoice,
they who are preeminent in performing the manifold acts such as creation; may those supreme ones who delight in all the Kula and Kaula traditions rejoice.
And others, through the distinctions of specific terms, [lead] to existence. || 7 ||
May the perfected masters rejoice, along with the successive lineages following them, the elders, the initiates, the young students, and the maidens,
born of the most eminent families of the six Yoginīs.
May the lords of the earth, the twice-born, and the virtuous people rejoice!

May those who are skilled in ethics, established in faultless conduct, free from envy, incomparable, and beyond description; who are eternal, devoted to the supreme joy, and desireless— may such gurus rejoice.
They were peaceful, with tranquil minds, their grief and fear removed.
May those devoted to yoga rejoice, as well as those joined to the family-yoga, the teachers, the initiates bound by the samaya, the practitioners, and the sons of the lineage;
may the cows, the twice-born, the young women, and the ascetics rejoice.
But your unwavering devotion to the Dharma and to your guru is singular. || 10 ||
May the lineages of practitioners established in powers such as *aṇimā* rejoice;
may the curses of the Yoginīs fall upon those who violate the covenant;
and may some indescribable power of Śambhu manifest.
For whom even the lotus-foot of that sprout is obtainable. || 11 ||
Those which reside in the wheels, the sequences, the stages, and the dwellings; those established within the channels;
those abiding in the pores of the body that emerge from the physical form; those situated within the elements;
those dwelling in the waves of the wind of the breath's surges; and those acting as the wind of exhalation.
May these goddesses, intent on devouring the faction of enemies and worshipped by the Kaulas, be satisfied. || 12 ||
Those goddesses who are born of the Kula, those deities dwelling on earth, those of eternally renowned splendor residing in fire, those who take refuge in the Mother,
those whose nature is the nectar of the sun’s orb in the sky, and those who are all-pervading at all times— [to them I bow].
May all those goddesses, devoted to the protection of the family path, grant me peace. || 13 ||
Whether above the cosmic egg, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the dry land, in the subterranean realms, in fire, in water, or in wind— wherever situated,
or having set foot even in the sacred fields (kṣetra), secondary fields (upakṣetra), and seats (pīṭha)— with incense, rows of lamps, and meat offerings;
May those goddesses, who are always pleased with us when the ritual of offerings is performed and who are worshipped by the lords of heroes, protect us. 14.
Brahmā, Śrī, Śeṣa, Durga, Guha, the Gaṇas, the Baṭukas, the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, the Guardians of the Directions,
Vetālas, Ādityas, Rudras, the Planets, Vasus, humans, spirits, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Ṛṣis, and gods.

The elephant-faced god (Gaṇeśa), all the deities residing within the body, the lords of the Kṣatriyas, the Bhairavas, the Yoginīs, the Baṭukas, the Yakṣas, the Pitṛs, the Bhūtas, the Piśācas, the Āgrahas,
and others who move on the earth, in the quarters, and in the sky— the Vetālas and the Ceṭakas— [are all present].
As the noble son drinks the beverage, [he eats] the sacrificial pap together with the lamp.

If the word of the Guru is indeed true; if the ancestors, the Vedas, the Agamas, and the Yoginis are pleased; if the Supreme Deity is indeed [my] refuge; if this Kaula system is indeed the authoritative vision; and if hope is indeed not in vain—then [act].
May Satyā, Sūryā, and the others of the Kaulika lineage be present upon the surface of the earth; may victory be mine forever. || 17 ||
May all the Mothers, the oceans, and the lords of their hosts, as well as the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas who reside within my body, be satisfied. (18)
May the universe—from Śiva down to the earth, including all from Brahmā to a blade of grass, and from Kālāgni up to Śiva—be satisfied by this sacrifice. (19)
Having thus recited the *śānti* and imparted the three principles (*tattvatraya*) to the disciple, one should recite the *saubhāgyahṛdaya*:
Oṃ, I bow to that supreme greatness, which is marked by the five activities.
Śiva, whose nature is the fullness of I-consciousness, is the self of all the manifold varieties of the universe without exception. || 1 ||
Salutation to that Great Splendor, the supreme eye, who is divided threefold according to the sequence of the hymn, the object of praise, and the act of praising.
I remember that supreme, immeasurable speech, which is the locus of primordial activity,
possessing manifold forms of thought, and embodying great majesty.
I take refuge in that digit of consciousness which manifests in whatever form—be it space, time, or substance—in whatever manner each respective object appears. (4)
I bow to that Mahātripurasundarī, the devourer of worldly existence, whose body is renowned as extending from the root-center (mūlādhāra) up to the crown of the head (bilapa).
O Great Goddess, your light shines like a mass of gold in the *yoni*, blazes like a flash of lightning in the heart, and resembles the moon in the *ājñā* [cakra]. 6.
I meditate upon Bhavānī, the Mistress of Nectar, whose flood of nectarous rays has completely satiated all that is moving and unmoving, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence.
O Goddess, the six paths— phoneme, the principle of the mother of the parts (kalā), word, and indeed the element— shine within you, the conscious Self.
O Mother, within you, whose very form is light, you unfold this wondrous and marvelous universe, beginning from Anāśrita up to Kālāgni and ending with Rudra.
O Goddess, that which shines forth here, consisting of name, form, and action, does not exceed You, whose very body is light. (10)
O Goddess, through the play of the lotus-throne of my heart, I repeatedly enjoy the honey of your form and other qualities, which arise from the network of your eyes and other features.
O Noble Goddess Saṃvid, having fully pervaded the objects of the senses, you always send them to the seat of nectar for the sake of the worship of yogins. 12.
"I consider neither what is desirable nor what is undesirable, nor even my own vital breaths;
O Pārvatī, O Queen of the Gods, you yourself must do whatever you deem right for me. (13)
The hymn *Saubhāgyahṛdaya* was composed by the yogi Citānanda for the sake of fulfilling his propitiation; it grants all desires. (14)
Thus has been composed this *Traipurastotra*,
which reveals the supreme reality, is honored by the best of yogis,
and performs the task of destroying all diseases and adversities.
Let it be resorted to by those endowed with devotion, according to the rules for each sacrifice. || 15 ||

Having recited this and lifted up the *śrīpātra*, one should satisfy it three times with the *pādukā* mantra as before; then, at the end of the root-vidyā, [one should offer] into that which blazes with internal, uninterrupted, and fuel-less combustion.
In this fire of consciousness, which is the adversary of the darkness of delusion and the ground for the expansion of some wondrous radiance,
I offer as an oblation the entire universe, from the earth to the very ends of the quarters.

One should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the mouth of the Supreme Deity, who is the nature of Kuṇḍalinī residing in the *mūlādhāra*, with the understanding that the substance has been placed in another vessel and accepted; this is the procedure for the dismissal of the venerable vessel (*śrīpātra*).
Then, having performed the remaining rites according to the method taught by the Guru, one should bring the ritual to completion. As it has been said:
In the *Svacchandapaddhati* (p.
274): "The Guru should offer the *śrīpātra* into the fire of consciousness by means of the three principles (*tattva*).
He should give the *gurupātra* to the Guru, and his own vessel to the disciple."
One should give the vessel of power to the Śakti, the vessel of enjoyment likewise to oneself,
and one should offer the vessel of the sacrificial oblation to the most excellent attendant.
One should purify the ground everywhere with conch water while reciting the mantra.
For one who has received the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking [the water] is correctly prescribed.
Having lifted the jar with both hands, one should drink the honey along with the second [offering];
taking the vessel with the hand, one should recollect the Mūlamantra and the Pādukā.
One should drink wine until the end of the *āmalaka* fruit; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for clearing the vessel.
Then, having filled a copper vessel with water mixed with fragrance, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers—
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! Salutations to Vivasvat, O Brahman, to the radiant one whose splendor is the universe;
salutations to Savitṛ, to Rudra, to Bhānu, the witness of all actions.
"Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ saḥ, to Sūrya, this is your arghya, svāhā! Having thus offered the arghya to Sūrya, [one should recite]:
"Whatever flaw there is in the sacrifice, whatever flaw in the austerity, whatever flaw in my worship—"
May all that be flawless through the grace of the Sun.

Then, having performed three breath-retentions (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, having prostrated to the Guru with "Śrīṃ," and having touched the remains of the offering (nirmālya) flower to one's head with the second kūṭa, one should give the food offering (naivedya) and other gifts to the devotees of the Supreme Deity;
then, having eaten together with other friends, one should contemplate oneself as transcending the universe.
Cultivating this, one may dwell in auspiciousness according to one's pleasure.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Svacchandapaddhati* composed by the illustrious Cidānandanātha.
Oṃ oṃ! May there be auspiciousness. The *Svacchandapaddhati* is completed. 99.
